en: Salutation to Śrī Sundaragaṇapati. {The Yogajāgama}

Salutations to the venerable Lord Somanātheśvara together with the venerable Amṛtāmbā. [Part 1] The installation of the retinue of the Yogaja-Tila; the characteristics of the preceptor (*ācārya*); the installation of Vighneśa; the installation of the *liṅga*; the installation of the jewel-*liṅga* (*ratnaliṅga*); the characteristics of the image (*pratimā*); the enumeration of *tāla* measures; the characteristics of stone (*śilā*). [Part 2] The hoisting of the banner (*dhvaja*); the procedure for the mandala (*maṇḍala*); the ritual for the ripening of fruits (*phalapāka*); the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣara*); the determination of wealth (*vibhava*); the procedure for the food offering (*naivedya*); the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*); the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*); the propitiatory oblation (*śāntihoma*).
(Section 3) The characteristics of initiation (*dīkṣā*). The characteristics of the temple (*prāsāda*). The characteristics of the *liṅga*.
(f.1a) I shall describe the installation of the retinue (*parivāra*) according to one’s means:
one should place the members of the retinue within the inner circle (*antarmaṇḍalaka*) in the eight [directions].
Alternatively, in another manner, or again within the interior,
one should place a bull in the inner circle and install it from the east.
Having brought the staffs from the pedestal— one, two, three, four, five, eight, nine,
up to ten and twelve— the bull, marked with the *piṅka* sign, is established. (3rd line) Having led the staffs from the pedestal, one installs the great bull upon the *khadyati*.
One may construct it with half the height of the temple, or indeed equal to the temple itself.
One should construct the inner mandala measuring three cubits;
the eight attendant deities are proclaimed to be according to the measurement of the interior of the wall.
Having established the constellation Aśvinī in the east and having milked [the vessel], one should place it with the Āgneya mantra.
Then, O Hero, one should station the seven groups of Mothers in the south.
One should place Gaṇanātha in the southwest, seated upon an elephant;
Saṅkumāra in the west;
Viṣṇu in the north; and likewise, one should install Caṇḍeśa from the northeast.
Having established [the deities] within the inner mandala, one should likewise arrange them right there.
Just as the great offering was made for the eight retinues,
one should lead the Kṣetrapāla to the center of the field of Yīśeya Indra.
In the inner mandala, in the northeast, one should fashion Caṇḍeśvara;
one should arrange sixteen attendants as the boundary-markers.
One should arrange Indra, Anila, and the world-protectors (Lokapālas) each in their respective places;
and [one should place] Vāgīśa, who is the size of a horse, upon a lotus wave.

One should install Jyeṣṭhā, the Lord of Serpents (Uragendra), Kṣetrapāla, and Ravi in sequence, ending in the directions of Indra, Agni, Vāyu, and Soma, and in the intermediate spaces. One should likewise station the doors at their respective locations, including the Samapāra and Vināśana.
Construct the residence for the retinue according to the measurement of the Āmalagarma.
Or it may be equal to half the temple, or even equal to half its inner sanctum;
this is prescribed by the rule for the width of the garland-pavilions (*mālā*).
One should fashion a pavilion with ten supporting pillars, a width of one *rasa* (six) units, and an interior space for the womb; it is desired that this have four doors and be the abode of the bull.
May Svasti-Durgā protect the dwelling; may she be the measure for the builders of the hall.
May she be the household for Guha, whose attendants are led by the elephant-headed Gaṇeśa.
In the northeast, one should fashion Hari in the form of a large lotus and Viṣṇukrāntā;
and in the north, Nandyāvarta, or else Caṇḍeśa and Bhāskara.
One should place the Bull upon the turret of the western gate,
and one should especially install Kumāra in the eastern region.
It may be located within a sūtra, or situated within a word, or it may be the abode of the retinue;
or for all the members of the retinue, it may simply take the form of a pavilion.
The celestial mansion may have the form of an assembly hall, or it may be shaped like a river;
its own abode-like form is within the range of vision of the lords of the fields of Kambu.
One should place the lords of the fields (īśānāḥ) within the boundary of the inner enclosure;
it is highly recommended that one arrange the retinue facing toward the temple.
Alternatively, one should have the retinue fashioned according to the characteristics of the images, so that they receive an equal share of the worship as all the other members of the entourage.
The bimba should be one-eighth [of the total height], while the pedestal should consist of one-sixteenth parts;
however, in the absence of an image, one should fashion a pedestal there instead.
One should establish it with a vimāna, or even without one;
it may be joined with a joint-winged base (sandhipakṣatāla), or even with a single tāla.
Its depth should be one-eighth of its width, or equal to its width;
it may have two tiers of moldings, or even just a single tier.
The girdle should be four fingers wide and consist of six lotuses;
one should fashion the pericarp with a measurement of one finger.
One should fashion the pedestal (piṭha) either circular or square;
when the installation of an image is to be performed, that [pedestal] must be made according to the requirements of the image.
[Thus ends the chapter on the ritual for the installation of the retinue in the Yogaja-pratiṣṭhā-tantra.]
Here, [the mantra] "Tāmbādhai namaḥ" (4th line).
Now, the installation of the Preceptor (ācāryasthāpana): I shall now describe the installation of the Preceptor in detail; listen.
The Śaiva, the Pāśupata, the Soma, and the Vākula are thus described.
Among these divisions of Śaivism, when [the initiates] have been initiated by whichever [division],
the rites such as installation (sthāpanā) and so forth must likewise be performed according to that single tantra.

Among these, one [text] is initiated; all are endowed with various positions. There is a single mantra, the Pāśupata, which is common to other tantras, yet divided in many ways—one, two, or more—into twenty [sections] among the *darbha* [manuscripts].
The consecration of the Tantras for the Pāśupata and other systems is now described.
Whatever has been commenced according to a particular tantra, one should carry that through to its conclusion according to that same tantra;
however, for the Anuttara [tantras], one should practice according to the principles of those tantras.
If a task has been undertaken by one person and, upon its completion,
it is performed by another, O Teacher, there would be a confusion of duties.
If an obstacle should arise during the performance of the ritual due to a deficiency in the qualities of the preceptor,
one should have that obstacle removed by his son or disciple, with his authorization.
Otherwise, that which is improperly performed destroys both the king and his kingdom; therefore, one should perform this destroyer of enemies exactly as it has been prescribed.
They are known as the Pañcaśailas, the Śaivasiddhāntins, and the Śaivakas;
namely, Kauśika, Kāśyapa, Bhāradvāja, and Gautama.
Agastya and these five others were initiated into the five faces;
Kāśyapa, however, was initiated into the form of Īśa and dwelt within the domain of Śiva.
The sage Bhāradvāja is indeed a form of Rudra; those initiated by him likewise [attain] the sphere of light, measured according to their respective order.
Gautama is a form of Viṣṇu, and his sphere is said to be the sky;
Agastya is a form of Brahmā, and therefore his sphere is the Sāvitrī.
In the Ādiśaiva-āgama it is stated: "The domain is called *kukha*;
one who is known among these *kula*s is fit for the rite of installation."
He who is called Ādiśaiva is the preceptor of Śiva and Brahmā;
having been initiated by Śiva himself, he is indeed termed Śivabrahmaṇa.
In the initiation of the Ādiśaiva, there are the Mahāśaivas and other Śaivas;
likewise, the initiated Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, along with their officiating priests.
(6th line) One may perform sacrifice for one's own sake, but not for the sake of another.
However, according to the Ādiśaiva [tradition], it should be performed both for one's own sake and for the sake of others.
The Mahāśaiva [receives] the portion of the Prāṇas;
the Anuśaiva, that of the Vaiśyas; and the Itathaiva, that of the Śūdras.
Among the Ādiśaivas and other Śaivas, the Mahāśaiva is declared to be the third [highest] guru.
Having bathed and performed the rites of *apanamaja* and so forth, one becomes an Ādiśaiva.
Any ritual act performed otherwise than prescribed is known as *ābhicāra* (malevolent magic).
Himavat, Kanyātīrtha, Antardhāna, Bhūmikṛṣṇa, and Mitabhava—[these are the sites].
There, by virtue of the excellent teacher [whose name begins with] *tra*, there were born those who followed the primary Śaiva tradition—
knowers of the reality of the Śaiva Siddhānta and devotees of the Lord who is the soul of the world.
He was a virtuous householder, of excellent character and pleasing appearance;
he wore his hair in the *śikhividdha* style and was free from the fatigue of physical exertion.
Born into an original Śaiva family, the status of a *mūrtipā* is proclaimed.
[Thus ends the chapter on the rules for the characteristics of an Ācārya in the *Pratiṣṭhātantra* by Yogaja.
Homage to the venerable Lord Somanātheśvara together with the venerable Amṛtāmbā.
The Installation of Vighneśa:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme installation of Vighneśa,
which bestows victory and liberation and increases one's sons and grandsons.
This merit, which increases the prosperity of the village and wards off all obstacles,
[is effective] in a village, a city, a town, and even a hamlet.
In Pūraṇa, Kubjaka, and especially in Rājadhānika,
the wise man should fashion the entrance and the temple in sequence,
beginning from three cubits and ending at nine cubits in size.
That which ought to be done must be done; beyond that, one should cause it to be performed.
In the eight directions, one should construct a palatial pavilion measuring one cubit in height. On its floor, one should fashion a door facing either east or north.

One should construct the enclosure wall and other features as before, using the measurement of the staff (*daṇḍa*). Whether at the front of the street, in the middle of the site, or near a shrine (*caitya*) or a well,
one should fashion the form of Vighneśvara (Gaṇeśa), which bestows all prosperity and happiness.
It is declared that [the direction] belonging to Indra bestows happiness, while those belonging to Agni are known to bestow wealth.
To the south of the house, slightly toward the southwest, is the *buddhivardhana* [plot];
the *rasasampatti* is in the west, and the *putravardhana* is in the northwest.
In the north it shall be the sign of wealth; in the northeast, it grants all desires.
At the front of the house, it is said to bring peace; in the center, it indeed bestows happiness.

And likewise, near a *caitya* tree or similar sites, it is supremely conducive to the increase of cattle. In this very manner, they should be worshipped in their respective places by the Lord of the Gaṇas.
Furthermore, the establishment of the primary [deities] and their association is declared to be twofold.
It is celebrated as being accompanied by its retinue and endowed with all its constituent parts.
One should begin the installation of the principal deity together with its retinue during the month of Āṣāḍha,
Kanyā (the month of Bhādrapada), or Mārgaśīrṣa.
One should especially avoid the months of Karkaṭaka and Mīna; however,
during the northern course of the sun (uttarāyaṇa), in the bright fortnight, on an auspicious day, the wise man should have an image fashioned according to the previously mentioned characteristics.
One should commence the installation on a Sunday or other such auspicious day.
The wise one should offer sprouts together according to the previously mentioned rite;
having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in the pavilion with pure and auspicious *śāli* rice.
One should place that above it; in its center, one should make [a space] like a cavity.
One should perform the fire-oblation with the Heart-mantra itself and install the [deities] in the maṇḍala in due order.
Having fashioned a mouse out of gold, one should place it in the central pit;
there, one should install the image, making it very smooth and very firm.
The arrangement of the clay [image], the half-brick [structure], and the half-canvas [representation],
as well as the placement of the jewels and the opening of the eyes.
One should perform the ritual of consecration in water, as well as the knowledge-rite, the lying down, and the installation, without the image,
according to the very same procedure prescribed for the installation of an image made of clay.
Then, on the day endowed with a pair of eyes (the second day), one should perform the opening of the eyes;
one should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with pure and auspicious *śāli* rice,
and place the image facing westward upon that mound.
With two strokes from a golden needle, one should draw the line of the wings.
Having drawn the seat-maṇḍala, one should draw the vision-maṇḍala;
having drawn the light-maṇḍala, the artisan should perform the dismissal.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) before that, one should place the image upon it.

Then, with the index, ring, and middle fingers, [one should place] the lords of the Sun, Moon, and Mars; and with the thumb and [other] fingers joined at the nails, they should be arranged in due order.
Having recited the Madhvājya Sūkta, one of sound intellect should display [the offerings] in the proper sequence.
Chanting the *Brahmasūkta* beginning with "yenāgāndharvaṃ dhanuḥ," he should remove the curtain while cutting through [the obstacles] and display himself to the assembly of people.
There, one should conquer the teacher by means of garments, gold, and finger-rings;
and one should bathe him with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), as well as with ghee and water.
[One should honor him] with clothes, ornaments, garlands, and such decorations as are worthy of adornment.
Accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments and adorned with every ornament.
Having performed a circumambulation of the village and entered it for the sake of water,
one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) on its bank and install the image there.
Having wrapped it in a new cloth and provided with a temple,
one should construct a water-shed in the middle of the water, adorned with four pillars,
equipped with a canopy and banners, and provided with a garland of *darśa* flowers.
Having boiled it in water that destroys throat ailments, [one should drink it] over a fruit.
Having stayed for one night, two nights, or three nights,
or having remained for a longer period, one should construct a pavilion with four doors and a pinnacle.

Having divided the pavilion into three parts, the sacrificial altar (vedikā) should be placed in the middle portion, provided with pillars made of uncarved wood and a hand-drawn opening for the Dharma.
One should subsequently prepare sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) one cubit in height, resembling the interior of a mirror,
at human intervals.
Alternatively, there may be nine fire-places or even five fire-places;
you should arrange the lotus-bowl-shaped pits in the cardinal directions and those shaped like horse-ears in the intermediate directions.
First, construct the principal circular pit in the center of the Kuṇḍalavedikā;
let it be known as the "five-fire" (pañcāgni) type, and one should avoid those shaped like a womb (yoni).
On the northern side of the pavilion, one should prepare a pit for the son-in-law...;
then, after dismissing the artisan, one should smear it with cow dung.
Having adorned the pavilion, one should then feed the Brahmins;
thereafter, one should smear the remains [of the offering] with cow dung.
Then, having performed the Vāstuhoma, carry out the rite of circumambulation with fire;
and having caused the proclamation of the auspicious day (Puṇyāha), accompanied by the Svasti-sūkta.
Equipped with a musical instrument held in the left hand and adorned with all ornaments,
one should have the deity emerge from the water and place him upon the bathing platform.
Then, having removed the garments and other items, one should perform the consecration with cow products alone;
having bathed [the image] with fragrant substances and so forth, one should offer a lamp at the feet.
Having worshipped with the Īśāna mantra, the wise one should wrap [the image] in a white cloth and bind the *kautuka* (protective thread) together according to the previously mentioned procedure.
To the north of the altar, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) using eight *droṇas* of rice;
having specifically strewn it with rice, sesame seeds, and *darbha* grass.
One should prepare a bed in the center with skins and musical instruments in due order;
one should sprinkle it with water using the *Puruṣasūkta* and the mantra beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*.
Accompanied by the teacher and the disciple, endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics,
wearing new garments and turbans, and adorned with golden rings;
having placed fuel on the bathing altar, fully equipped with all ornaments.
O Queen of the Lord of the Bedchamber, one should worship Vighneśa with the mantra "śanno devī".
Having laid it down, the mantra-practitioner should then worship it from the east, the north, and the top;
thereafter, having performed the rites with water, he should envelop it with a red cloth.
Having displayed the lotus mudrā, one should then display the one called Amśuka;
endowed with all the characteristics, one should arrange it according to the Kuṭila Tantra.
With its lid and spout, covered with cloth and filled with water,
one should place it as prescribed by the preceptor in the north-eastern direction of the Lord of Obstacles (Vighneśa).
In that very place, one should deposit the five jewels with the *hṛdaya-mantra*;
one should install Gaṇeśa in the middle of the pitcher with the root mantra.
The letter *kha* joined with the letter *ta*, the letter *ya* conjoined with the letter *ta*,
and [the letter] joined with the end of the thirteenth [vowel], conjoined with the sixtieth vowel.
This is declared to be the root mantra of Vighneśa; it becomes victorious when joined with the letter at the end of "kha" (the letter *ha*). One should then fashion the Brahma-limbs [of the deity].
Gaṇeśa, who has the form of a man, with the ears and face of an elephant,
possessing a large belly and a massive body— ending thus— is the three-eyed one.
With fierce eyes and protruding lips, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread,
adorned with a crown-case (karaṇḍa) diadem, and beautified by all ornaments.
Endowed with four arms, he holds a *kuśa* stalk in his right hand,
while on his left side he bears a noose and a sweetmeat ball (*laḍḍuka*).
Having meditated upon this form of Gaṇeśa, which possesses the trunk of an elephant's nose and is established in the palm of the hand, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of that form.
Having worshipped them with perfumes and other offerings, one should display the five mandalas,
filled with half a droṇa of water and provided with threads and other requisites.
One should place eight water-pots, filled with scented water and equipped with golden nooses and goads, in the eight directions, [each] adorned with the [eight] fear-dispelling goddesses.
One should worship Varada in the eastern pitcher, Virama in the southeastern pitcher,
Vighnesha in the southern pitcher, and Gajanana in the southwestern pitcher.
One fond of food should worship Vāruṇī in the west; likewise, Gajakarṇa in the northwest;
Vināyaka in the north; and Lambauṣṭha should be worshipped in the northeast.
Now the specific details are being stated, all of which are like the form of Vighneśa:
the Lord holding a noose and a goad, endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons.

Having meditated upon them as having two eyes and two hands, one should place them within the pitcher with their respective seed-syllables (bījas) and worship them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
One should cause rice mixed with jaggery to be given to them, and the preceptor should cause betel-leaf to be offered.
One should place eight surrounding jars upon the secondary altar;
[they should be filled with] white, black, green, dark-blue, red, yellow, saffron,
and the brilliant color known as *dhīmavarṇa*.
And those of terrifying form, with tusks, holding swords and shields in their hands.
Adorned with all ornaments, with hair standing erect and marked by the letter *la*,
they have two eyes, dark faces, and are endowed with the first syllable of their respective names.
One should worship them especially with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, in due order.
For the two door-protectors, one should place [vessels] on the side-altars (upavedī).
These should be filled with water, covered with lids, and wrapped in cloth.
The yellow [color] is on all sides, while the red is on the left side.
Having two arms and two eyes, with the left and right [hands] holding a *dā* and a *dhara*;
having fanned [the fire] with one's own breaths, one should place the *namaḥ* [mantra] in the lower part.
Having consecrated with mantras recited from the heart, one should perform the study of the directions in sequence, beginning with the east and so forth, using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
The entire procedure for the installation of the fire (agnyādheya) should be performed according to the path prescribed for fire-rituals;
having prepared the fire for Gaṇeśa, one should distinguish it according to the specific sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Having prepared sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, and various ritual implements according to the prescribed rules.
First, [one should place] a branch of the *godu* tree, and likewise a *prathuka*,
a *panasa*, a *śami*, a *khadira*, an *āyūra*, and an *udumbara* in the cardinal directions.
The Bilva, Akṣa, Plakṣa, and Nyagrodha trees are for the intermediate directions;
however, the Palāśa is proclaimed as the primary fuel for the principal fire.
One should offer the sacrificial materials, such as fuel-sticks and clarified butter, in sequence with their respective mantras,
one hundred times, fifty times, or twenty-five times for each, in due order.
Having offered the *vyāhṛti* oblation at the end of the materials, one should, without touching [the central image], offer to the images in sequence;
then, having touched and untouching the guardians of the forms (*mūrtipās*) in their respective directions, one should perform the *homa*.
The preceptor, repeatedly touching the ground,
should perform the oblation with the mantra "gaṇānām tvā" and especially with the root mantra.
The practitioner of mantra should offer oblations for each [deity], with a hundred offerings for each;
thus, having kept vigil through the night, he should do so when the dawn is clear.
There, one should honor the preceptor with garments, gold, and rings;
afterwards, one should cause a sacrificial fee to be given along with cows, land, and gold.
Five niṣkas should be known as the minimum; double that is the middle amount, and triple that is declared to be the fee for the preceptor.
One should worship the forms of the reciters according to the prescribed ritual;
then, with firmness, one removes the bedding and the cloth and other coverings from the image.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth; then one should worship the jars.
Afterwards, one should worship the fire, specifically directed toward the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍala).
One should then shake [the vessel] in sequence, performing the Jaya-homa and other rites, as well as the Abhyadhāna and the Rāṣrabhra.
And having offered the full oblation with the mantra "The fire has been well-sacrificed by me," one should then dismiss the fire and commence the installation.
Having lifted Gaṇeśa from his bed with the ritual services of bathing and the sacrificial altar,
one should establish the retinue within the center of the inner maṇḍala.
Having first prepared a very abundant sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha),
the wise practitioner should place it with that mantra and worship it in due order.
One should install [the deities] in due order, beginning with oneself and proceeding clockwise.
I shall now describe the procedure for daily worship, which is supreme and brings about all accomplishments.
Having bathed according to the prescribed rule, perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa;
then, having gathered the materials for worship, one should sprinkle them with the Puruṣa-sūkta.
Having brought them to the doorway, one should worship the two door-keepers;
then Lakṣmī above the lintel and Pṛthivī below it.
Having performed worship according to the rule, he should enter from the beginning to the end;
then, having performed purification through bathing, as well as by means of sprinkling, smearing, and so forth.
Then, having performed the purification of the vessels, one should purify the ritual substances according to their nature;
after the worship is completed, one should dismiss everything with the heart-mantra.
One should fashion the image from stone, metal, or wood;

in the case of a painted image or a wooden figure, one should perform the purification of the image (*bimbaśuddhi*). Having performed the purification with pure water according to the specific requirements of purity...
One should then prepare the seats in the directions starting from the southeast (Agni) and so forth.
Knowledge of the Dharma, detachment, and heterogeneity are the supports;
unrighteousness is said to be the pill, located in the directions of worship and so forth, beginning with the east.
Having consecrated it with the three qualities, one should place the seat above it—
a lotus consisting of nine syllables, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise.
One should place the letters beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa* upon the eight petals;
one should worship the syllable *oṃ* in the pericarp with perfumes and flowers.
Above all [this], one should worship the elephant-faced [deity] outside with the *Sadyojāta* mantra.
Having meditated upon that form of subjugation, one should perform the ritual bath with the root mantra.
Now, one should offer water for the feet with the *sadyojāta* mantra, and the *manīyaka* (garland) with the *śiras* mantra;
there, one should cause the *arghya* and the fragrance to be offered with the *śiva* mantra.
One should especially cause a lamp to be offered with the armor-mantra (kavaca). For each substance, one should offer the water for sipping (ācamanīya), consecrated with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
One should install the eight forms beginning with Varada upon the eastern petal and the others;
one should worship them with their respective initial syllables using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
One should offer wine, meat, fish, or pure food.
Having offered to the God gum-vāṣa together with galopeta and upadaṃśa, as well as ripe fruits indeed; (f. 7b)
One should offer [the oblation] to Vighneśa with the mantra "gaṇānāṃ tvā," and the wise person should present the subsidiary offerings and the bali with their respective mantras.
In the fire of youth, one should especially fashion an earring— whether circular or square— and then perform the oblation (*homa*) as a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the fire.
Thereafter, one should offer water for sipping (*ācamana*), having first removed the food offering (*naivedya*).
The preceptor should cause betel-leaf to be offered to him with his own mouth;
thereafter, he should worship [the deity] daily at four times or three times.
The wise man should maintain the perpetual fire, especially within the *yauvanāgni*.
One should fashion the sacrificial pit there, either circular or square.
Then one should perform the fire-oblation (homa), preceded by the consecration of the fire;
one should offer clarified butter with the Vāmadevya mantra and offer food with the Sadyojāta mantra.
There should be ten oblations for each of the five Brahmans and the six parts;
and the best of preceptors should likewise perform the Vyāhṛtis at the end of the substances.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) once, twice, or thrice a day;
at its conclusion, one should hold a festival accompanied by ten thousand recitations of the Vighneśa-pratama.
The length is prescribed as being equal to eleven finger-breadths (rudrāṅgula).
And the middle one is proclaimed to have an extent equal to nine finger-breadths.
The form of Vighneśa should be fashioned according to the characteristics described for images.
In this manner, perform the consecration as before, up to half of the daily festival.
Then, one should have the installation performed for [the image] adorned with all ornaments.
Having summoned an attendant who wears a turban and has his ears pierced,
the wise man should place Vighneśa upon the crown of that person's head.
It was provided with all kinds of musical instruments and accompanied by yak-tail whisks.

The Lord of all sciences, the Sovereign of all beings,
the Overlord of Brahman, the Overlord of the sacred word— may that Brahman be auspicious to me.

"May there be *sadāśivaṃ namaḥ*," having bound [the mudrā] upon the head of Īśāna with the tip of the thumb in the *bhadra-mudrā*. Then, with the application of the index finger and thumb, one should place [the mantra] on the face of Tatpuruṣa, reciting: "We know that which belongs to Tatpuruṣa; we meditate upon Mahādeva; may Rudra impel us. Next, with the application of the middle fingers, one should perform the *aghora-astra-tantra*, reciting: "Oṃ, to the non-terrible ones... to the forms. Finally, with the joining of the ring fingers, one should perform the *vāmadeva* [mudrā], reciting: "Salutation to Vāmadeva... salutation to Manonmanā. Thus, by means of Vāmadeva...

O Guhyaka! *Oṃ sadyojātaṃ prapadyāmi... bhavāya namaḥ*. Thus, by means of the little finger (*kaniṣṭhāṅguli*), having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the limb of Brahmā known as Sadyojāta—which is the ground of the form of the all-pervading Self (*vyāpakātman*)—starting from the feet up to the crown of the head; then, in the upward, eastern, southern, northern, and western directions, and by way of various artistic arrangements (*citrabhaṅgyā*) and modal arrangements (*kalābhaṅgyā*): "To Īśāna, the Lord of all sciences (*sarvavidyānām*), obeisance to Śaśinī" on the uppermost head; "To Īśvara, the Lord of all beings (*sarvabhūtānām*), obeisance to Aṅgadā."

(5th line) On the eastern head: *Āṃ*, obeisance to Brahmādhipati, to the Lord of Brahmā, to Brahmā-Rudrā. On the southern head: *Brahmā-śivo me astu*, obeisance to Marīci. On the northern head: *Oṃ*, obeisance to Sadāśiva-Jvālīnī. (6th line) On the western head: thus is the pentad of the Īśāna-kalās. To the upper face, which is the syllable *Praṇava*: obeisance to the Unmanifest Kalā (*Avyakta-kalā*). To the Puruṣa, we offer our meditation; obeisance to Śānti. (7th line) To the eastern face, to Mahādeva, we offer our meditation; obeisance to Vidyā.

Thus, on the southern face: *Oṃ tanno rudra pratiṣṭhāyai namaḥ*. On the northern face: *Oṃ pracodayān nivṛttyai namaḥ*. On the western face: [the five-fold *kalā* of Tatpuruṣa] *Aghorebhyo namaḥ*, *Māyāyai namaḥ*. In the heart: *Oṃ aghoratarebhyo mohāyai namaḥ*. On the neck: *Oṃ aghorarakṣāyai namaḥ*. On the right shoulder: *Ghoratarebhyo niṣṭhāyai namaḥ*. On the left shoulder: *Oṃ sarvataḥ sarva mṛtyave namaḥ*.

At the navel: *Oṃ*, salutation to all [forms] of Māyā; at the belly: *Oṃ*, salutation to you, Bhavā; at the hips: salutation to Jarā, who has the form of Rudra. Thus is the group of eight parts of Bahurūpa. At the chest: *Oṃ*, salutation to Vāmadeva, salutation to Jarā; at the secret place: *Oṃ*, salutation to Jyeṣṭha, salutation to Rakṣā; at the penis: *Oṃ*, salutation to Rudra, salutation to Ratī; on the right thigh: salutation to Kalā, salutation to Pālyā; on the left thigh: salutation to Kalakāmā; on the right knee: [salutation to Balakālī].

Oṃ *vikaraṇāyanamassaṃyamanyai* namaḥ, on the left knee; Oṃ *hiṃ balakriyāyai* namaḥ, on the right calf; Oṃ *vikaraṇāyanamo budhyai* namaḥ, on the left calf; Oṃ *hiṃ balakāryai* namaḥ, on the right buttock; Oṃ *pramadhanāya namodhātrai* namaḥ, on the left buttock;
Oṃ *hiṃ sarvabhūtadanayāya namo bhrāmiṇyai* namaḥ, on the waist; Oṃ *mohinyai* namaḥ, on the right side.

Oṃ hiṃ, salutation to Unmanā; salutation to Bhavā—thus on the left side are the thirteen kalās of Vāmadeva. Oṃ, I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutation to Siddhi. On the right foot: salutation to Sadyojātā; salutation to Vṛddhi. On the left foot: Oṃ haṃ, salutation to Bhavadyuti. On the right hand: Oṃ haṃ, salutation to Bhavalakṣmī. On the left hand: Oṃ, salutation to Anādibhava-medhā. On the nose: Oṃ haṃ, salutation to Bhajasvamāṅkāñji.

On the head: *oṃ haṃ bhavasvadhāyai namaḥ*. On the right arm: *oṃ haṃ utbhavāya namaḥ*. On the left arm: *dhṛtyai namaḥ*. Thus is the eightfold *kalā* of Sadyojāta. Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the thirty-eight *kalās*, beginning with Īśāna, along with their respective mudrās, one should worship the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*). Having invoked the root mantra, one should [place] the heart-mantra on the heart, the head-mantra on the head, the crest-mantra on the crest, and the armor-mantra on all the mantras.

Having rendered weapon after weapon upward with the Great Mudrā (*mahāmudrā*) and having planted them with three *tāla*-claps and a snap of the fingers, one should perform the expulsion of the obstacles of those deities by means of the Weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*), illuminating the directions with the index fingers. One should place *Oṃ Kāṃ* on the head; one should place the Root-mantra (*mūla*) on the forehead. One should place *Oṃ Raṃ* on the two eyes, and *Um* on the two ears. One should place *Ṛg* on the two shoulders, and *Ḷḷ* on the two nostrils. *E Ai* are on the two lips; *O Au* are on the two rows of teeth.
Having placed [the letters] upon both lips and also upon both rows of teeth, one should place them within the palate; starting from the right in due order, they are arranged sequentially.
A wise person should place the syllables beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa*.
In the head, the forehead, the face, the two ears, and the two cheeks.
One should place the vowels upon her two lips, both rows of teeth, the tongue, the palate, and the lower lip; and the consonants (vyañjanas) below them.
The *ka*-group [of consonants] is on the right hand, and the *ca*-group is on the left hand;
the *ṭa*-group is on the right feet, and the *ta*-group is on the left foot.
One should place the *pavarga* on the right side and the *bhavarga* on the left side;
one should place the letter *ma* in the region of the ears and at the base of the shoulders.
Having deposited the skin, blood, flesh, fat, marrow, and semen, [one should place the letters].
One should arrange [the letters] beginning with *ṣa* and ending with *sa* in their proper sequence.
Having placed the syllable *haṃ* in the heart and the syllable *la* on the two testicles,
one should especially place the syllable *kṣa* in the region of the anus.

He is in a state of meditative absorption, possessing the luster of jasmine, the moon, and crystal, and wears a crown of matted locks; from the head downward, his five faces are endowed with fifteen eyes.
Adorned with all ornaments and endowed with ten arms,
he holds a trident, an axe, a sword, and a thunderbolt in his right hands, along with the gesture of fearlessness.
In the left [hands], he holds a noose, a serpent, a goad, a bell, and fire;
together with the limbs of Sadyojāta, the left face should be red in appearance.
The Person who resembles collyrium yet is not terrible, who has the luster of saffron and is like pure crystal— He is called the Pure Īśāna.
I perpetually bow to Sadāśiva, who has the appearance of cow’s milk in whiteness,
the divine Lord wearing celestial garments and adorned with celestial flowers.
With limbs anointed with divine perfumes, possessing a tranquil form and a mindful countenance,
standing, sitting, or reclining, with two feet upon a seat—
thus one should install the form of Sadāśiva within the Śivaliṅgas.
She has two eyes and two arms, with broad hips, a large posterior, and full breasts.
Adorned with all ornaments, dark-complexioned, smiling and gracious,
the goddess holds a lotus and a water-lily, and is embellished by her flowing locks of hair.
Adorned with a crown and a casket, with a red cloth as an upper garment,
the divine form of the god Vāmana is beyond the reach of the mind.
O Goddess, one should recite thus and perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the two-footed [deity] seated upon a lotus;
or else, one should meditate upon it in another manner by means of the four arms.
Having first meditated thus upon the one who grants fearlessness and boons, who is adorned with supreme flowers, seated upon his throne, and possessing feet, hair, and so forth—
[as well as] sandals, shoes, and shanks in this world.
They say the womb is the kumuda, and it is indeed blossomed by the two arms.
The *karṇakarṇa* is said to be the *madharammarapaṭṭikā*;
the *mahāpaṭṭi* is to be known as the *mukha*, and the *śirovṛtti* is the *vārikā*.
Having meditated upon [the deity] as endowed with such characteristics, the wise one should place the mind;
and from the linga, he should assign a portion in the eighth part and assign each portion accordingly.
It is said that three parts constitute the head, and three parts likewise the thighs;
three parts are said to be the body, while the neck is declared to be one part.
One should place two parts for the head-covering and two parts for the face;
such is the stated characteristic, and one should fashion all the lingas accordingly.
A linga that remains in its current state is superior to Śiva for a month.
The square-shaped bed, the svastika, and the liṅga-puṅgaka;
One should study and meditate upon the *liṅga* endowed with these characteristics:
Gaurī is seated upon a circular pedestal, while [the deity] sits upon an auspicious throne (*bhadrapīṭha*).
The bed should be upon a lotus pedestal; on other [pedestals], it may be moving or stationary.
However, the *nandyāvarta* [bed] with a pedestal should be like gold, possessing four faces, four arms, and [holding] a rosary, a water-pot, and a staff.
One should fashion the connection between the two hands above the penis and the cow-hide.
It is recited in the sequence of up, down, right, and left;
having established it upon a tortoise-shaped stone, O Goddess Earth, with a mind possessing the auspicious marks.
Having meditated thus in the mind upon [the deity] who has two arms, is white in appearance, and is seated upon Ananta, one should then perform the ritual installation.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should consecrate [the object] with a portion of Śiva;
then, having performed the binding of the directions (digbandha), one should display the lotus mudrā (padmamudrā).
One should show the five-faced deity called Liṅga for purification with the Surabhi-mudrā,
specifically above the Liṅga with the Heart-mantra.
One should likewise show the Padma-mudrā over the entire Pīṭha, especially.
Having kindled the fire at the proper time, one should perform the oblation from time to time.

One should perform the Jaya and other offerings, as well as the Rāṣṭrabhṛt and the Abhyātāna oblations; and one should offer the Pūrṇāhuti with the head [of the ladle], reciting the mantra beginning with "sviṣṭakṛte".
Then, after the conclusion of the fire sacrifice (homa), the jar, together with the preceptor and the image-keepers,
should be placed upon a pedestal adorned with all ornaments and two variegated banners;
it should be provided with incense and lamps and carried on the head.
Then, the preceptor, holding the auspicious water-pot (śivakumbha), [should recite] the root mantra at the end.
Then the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) should hold the water-pot (kumbha) and the prosperity-vessel (vardhanī).
Having lifted the pot with their heads, they should perform a circumambulation of the temple (dhāma).
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) at the tip of the liṅga and filled it with rice grains,
one should place Sadāśiva upon the mound and meditate upon him.
Having firmly established him as the deity, one should perform the rite of confinement (nirodhana) with the Aghora mantra.
But by a man, it should face toward Īśāna while he himself remains in proximity.
Having meditated upon the mantra in the *amanonmanī* state, especially within the *piṇḍikā*,
one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantra during an auspicious conjunction and at a favorable moment.
The preceptor, with a serene mind, standing to the right of the *liṅga*,
should begin the installation after understanding the yoga of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
That which is called the "vital breath mantra" is the principle, and that which is called "primordial nature" is the rule.
Having invoked the seed-syllables of the jars, one should diligently invoke them in the proper sequence.
With the right hand, one should place [the drop] upon the crown of the head;
joined with meditative concentration, one should always recollect it.
The wise should place each limb together with the limbs of the root mantra upon every limb;
one should deposit the thirty-eight digits (kalās) starting from the crown of the head down to the feet.
Having meditated upon the form of Sadāśiva, one should worship with the *kumbhottaka* (the water-pot).
Having invoked the water into the *vardhanī* vessel, one should place it upon the pedestal to the left;
then, having established that water upon the pedestal, the wise practitioner should perform the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*).

One should worship the assembly of Vidyeśvaras and the world of Indra and the other [deities] according to the path of the five enclosures (pañcāvaraṇa); thus the prescribed worship should be well-performed.
Having offered the oblation specifically with five colors and five faces by means of the path of the five obscurations,
one should perform all other rites as prescribed for worship.
One should honor the service and worship of those who are devoted to the teacher and the disciple.
[Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for the installation of the *liṅga* in the *Yogaja-pratiṣṭhā-tantra*. Homage to the illustrious Somanātheśvara together with the illustrious Amṛtāmbā.
Now, the installation of the jewel-*liṅga* (and the metal *liṅga*).
Hereafter, I shall describe the installation of the jewel-*liṅga* and that of the one made of metal.
The two months of Āṣāḍha, and Maghā and Mārgaśīrṣaka.
The months that are not recommended and those that are recommended for one who is well-conducted:
in all the excellent months, during the bright fortnight, on an auspicious day.
One should commence the installation on an auspicious weekday conjoined with a favorable asterism,
either nine or seven days prior to the day of the consecration.
On the fifth day, one should plant all the sprouts according to the previously mentioned procedure in a pure,
auspicious, and beautiful location, such as a temple or even a house.
One should extract the splinter (śalya) there; a pavilion (maṇṭapa) is constructed as before.
Then follow the depositing of jewels (ratnanyāsa), the opening of the eyes (akṣimokṣa), and the preliminary consecration with water (jalādhivāsa).

One should worship the jewel-liṅga (*ratnaliṅga*) precisely according to the sequence prescribed for worship. One-third of the liṅga itself should likewise serve as the pedestal (*pīṭha*). Thus, it is endowed with all the auspicious characteristics. [Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for the installation of the jewel-liṅga in the *Yogaja-pratiṣṭhā-tantra*.]
Salutations to the venerable Somanātheśvara, accompanied by the venerable Amṛtāmbā. Now, I shall specifically describe the characteristics of images;
listen. [The Characteristics of Images] Now, I shall describe in detail the characteristics of images; listen.
That which is both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*) is called the *Vairantamāta*.
From the pillar (*stambha*), there is the *adhiṣṭhāna*, the door, and the goddesses;
these are the best, the middling, and the lowest, consisting of nine portions.
Each one is eightfold by its ritual function and ninefold according to its specific manifestation;
the measurement of the *liṅga* is thirty-three, with ten being the length and width.
One should not treat with such pride either a virtuous man or a sage;
these five, however, are the extensions of the eleven-fold pride.
There would be thirty-three divisions according to the sequence from top to bottom; the measurement of others would be by the measure of the *liṅga*, but for the rest, it would be unobtainable.
I shall describe the measurement of the hand, beginning with one and ending with nine jewels; having established the measurement, it is now stated in finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
The five jewels should have a height of one hundred [units] or more as appropriate;
according to the measurement of the principal image, it should be twenty-four [units] greater.
The measurement is the length of the root finger; that measurement is the determination of the measure.
[It is taken] from the middle of the middle finger of the sacrificer’s right hand.

One should have that divine [image] made from parvata-wood or āyava-wood according to the measure of the mother-finger (mātrāṅgula). One should fashion the height of the planets according to their middle position.
Among the three measures of three fingers each, a person of noble birth should not disregard the Śaka [measure].
One should act likewise when measuring; however, one should plant a genuine Śaka tree.
Eighty-four [units] plus two parts of sixty-one,
(f.21a) and a hundredth part, as well as a sixteenth part.
One should deposit one part with effort, according to the sequence starting with the Brāhmaṇas;
thus is the share of the kinsmen declared, and its measure is indeed the wealth.
If it is joined with an auspicious measure, one should cause the Āya and other factors to be proclaimed.
One should divide that which measures from thirty up to one hundred by the number [of deities].
One should bind each [digit] there for the occurrence of fortune and so forth;
the beginning of the life-span (āya) is declared to be the Śaka year, and one should determine the six [periods] in its division.
Having determined the Berayāma with the [eight] qualities of Sundarī,
one should extract it from the heart in due order, consisting of ten [syllables] with the Sun as the tenth and possessing eight splendors.
If the remaining income exceeds the expenditure, it is auspicious;
if the expenditure exceeds it, there is loss of grain; if they are equal, it is said to be middling.
In the three birth-stars, the asterism of the elephant (Jyeṣṭhā), and the auspicious Daṇḍa-pada,
the feet of the wise, the donkey, and the crow bring about the destruction of what has been accomplished.
The wise know that the previous measure should again be taken up by means of eight cognitions;
and when divided by twenty-seven, the remainder of six, five, and so forth, is obtained.
An even number is said to bring all happiness, while an odd number brings unhappiness to people;
one should especially avoid being honored as a leader of a group.
One should avoid the eighth lunar day and the eighth mansion; if the eighth mansion falls on the eighth lunar day, destruction will befall the patron who is engaged in the rite.
Where there is happiness for the kingdom and its subjects, conducive to the king’s welfare,
he should protect the heart of the realm from thieves and other dangers by means of the four [measures].
The thief, the one with the power of enjoyment, the fortunate one, the one who casts down kings,
the one devoid of existence, the poor man, and the one called "well-kindled"— these are the nine types of Śakas. Among them, one should avoid both the utterly destitute and the thief.
Then, one should divide that by the sages multiplied by the height and the joy.
On a Sunday, one should avoid the *dārasaura* (the conjunction of Venus and Saturn).

[Thus ends the chapter on the rules for the characteristics of images in the *Yogayogī-pratiṣṭhā-tantra*. Salutations to the venerable Somanātheśvara, accompanied by the venerable Amṛtāmbā. [The number of] *tāla*s...
Now I shall explain in detail the rules for the number of *tālas*;
that which is taught as ranging from ten *tālas* down to one is called the *darśya-tāla*.
The best [image] should be ten tālas, which is twenty-four aṅgulas;
the middle is one hundred and twenty, and the smallest is sixty-six.
The *jyeṣṭha* [type] consists of one hundred and twelve *tanmātras* with nine *tālas*;
the *madhyama* consists of one hundred and eight; and the *adhama* consists of ninety *tālas*.
Just as in sequence, [the image] consisting of four measures is for a single deity;
the supreme [image] for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara is ten tālas in height.
With the pride that arises from the conviction that [the sacrifice] must be performed, he offered oblations in due order;
at that very moment, Umā, Sarasvatī, and the other goddesses emerged from the middle limb.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Vaiṣṇavī,
Varāhakī, Kaumārī, Cāmuṇḍī, Īśvarī, and Aparājitā.

And of all the weapons of the eldest [deities], as well as those of the Kṣetrapālas, [the measurement] is likewise by ten *tāla*s of the youngest; the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) follows the sequence of the path.
Āditya, Skanda, Indra, Mohinī, and Nayanā; likewise Abhicaṇḍeśvara, Yama, Aśva, Varuṇa, and Vāyu.
Śvāpi, Kubera, Gandharva, Yakṣa, Rākṣasa, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Nāgas, and the hosts of Vidyādharas—
these, along with Garuḍa and Matya, are among the elders of Navatālaka.
In the middle [section], with a span of nine tālas, are the Vidyeshas and likewise the Śruti.
One should likewise conceive of the remaining [deities] as being neither middling nor low;
the seven Rohiṇīs and the Piśācas are middling, measuring eight tālas.
The height of the *kubjaka* [type of pillar] is six *tālas*, while others in the group have five *gālas*;
likewise, the *vāmana* should be thus, and the *bhuktaka* is four *sthālas*.
The Kinnaras and horses are three tālas; the Kūṣmāṇḍas are two tālas;
the Kabandhas are one tāla; thus they know the sequence of the Revanta tālas.
One should divide the measurement of the image by means of the palm-span;
the wise man should make that into equal parts, which is called a *gulikā*.
One part out of those [sixteen] parts is proclaimed to be one *aṅgula*;
eight *yavas* are said to constitute an *aṅgula*, and by that measure one should calculate [the dimensions].
The portion for the throat and neck should be two, three, or four finger-breadths; the color should be the measure of barley-grains, and the face should be twelve measures.
The face of Yama-tāla measures twelve vitastis;
this constitutes the measurement (māna), the dimension (pramāṇa), the height (unmāna), the measurement of the image (bimbamāna), and the proportionate measure (umānaka).
The supreme image (bera) should be fashioned with five times that measurement;
its size is said to be equal to the circumference of the [image's] neck.
The measurement that extends to the tip of the nose is established as the *pramāṇa*;
however, when it is shorter than that, it is proclaimed as the *māna* of the gods.
The power that has the Vedas as its cause is known as "the hanging thread";
it is proclaimed as the incomparable means by which the states of being low, high, and mad are destroyed.
The uṣṇīṣa is said to be one aṅgula; the measurement of the hair (keśa) shall be one kalā. From the end of the hair to the limit of the sūtra, and from there to the tip of the nose.
The portion from the nose to the end of the nostrils is thus described;
the portion extending the length of the neck is that which lies from the base of the neck to the end of the breasts.
The foot should constitute one part; thus the measurement has been declared.
Having omitted [the proportions] from the ankles, knees, and crown of the head, one should increase them in the other parts.
Whatever remains, the wise man should distribute accordingly; that which is here [stated] should be decreased by three.
His upper body was made of iron, while his lower body was entirely endowed with auspicious marks.
Whether less, more, or equal, this [measurement] shall be auspicious for all.
The measurement of the ram has thus been indicated; now the proportions are being described.
The width is twelve parts; as proclaimed for the first three starting from the face, the peaceful [portion] at the back from the uṣṇīṣa is said to be twelve finger-breadths.
From the crown of the head (uṣṇīṣa) to the forehead, the distance is prescribed as nine units (mātras); from the crown to the side of the head, it is one unit less, namely eight units.
The distance between the two ears is prescribed as twenty units.
From the tip of the nose to the ears, it is said to be twelve finger-breadths in length.
The distance from the ears to the back [of the head] should be twelve and a half mātrās;
the width of the *kolakarṇa* should be twice its length.
The bridge extending from the tip of the ear should be half a finger-breadth;
the two ears should have a width of one finger-breadth, and that [area] along with the ears is the fillet (*paṭṭikā*).
The ear-stalk is one finger-breadth in measure;
the ear is shaped like the letter *la*; the binding, the pedestal, and the crest-fiber are likewise formed.
The width is half a mātrā and a finger-breadth, endowed with a thickness of half a mātrā;
the two tubes, extending from east to west, are proclaimed as being suspended from the divisions.
From the outer corner of the eye to the root of the ear, that distance is proclaimed to be seven finger-breadths (saptamātra).
One's own natural height is six finger-breadths, and the kola, the ear, and the eye are each remembered as one finger-breadth.
With five [fingers] in between, one should request the measure of the light;
the sacrificial staff (yaṣṭi) should have the appropriate measurement and be made of Karavīra wood.
It is of three kinds—white, red, and black—and resembles the eye.
Because he has ninety hairs on each side of his body, his face resembles the hub of a wheel.
Between the eyebrows and the sutra, two nail-lengths are elevated;
above the circle of the eyebrows is the peaceful [state], which is thoroughly understood as such.

The length of the eyebrows is one-and-a-half finger-breadths; their width is said to be two [finger-breadths] by Yamī. Furthermore, the breadth at the top and bottom of the eyebrow is one and a half barley-corns.
The space between the two eyebrows should be two mātras; the brow-line (bhrū-sakti), along with its limb, is one aṅgula.
From the base of the goji (the outer corner of the eye), extending two mātras, there is the elevation of the nose.
From the two nostrils, it should project like a flower, and likewise, it should be shaped like a *vākolaka* fruit.
The shaft should have a width of five finger-breadths and a height of five barley-corns.
The height of the Puṣkara is said to be six yavas;
likewise, its width at the top for a male is proclaimed to be the same measure.
The tip of the nose, shaped like a sesame flower and adorned with a *yava* grain, should be placed at the base of the nose at a height equal to its own measure; this is what is called [the posture].
From the corner of the mouth to the edge of the lower lip, it is measured at four mātrās including the *vayaṃkola*; the height of the upper lip is prescribed as one additional [mātrā].
The width of the upper lip is proclaimed to be three [mātrās].
There, a small bowl was filled with barley, especially for the sake of Vikrama.
The depth at the gojī is four yavas, and it is depressed by one and a half yavas;
its width at the gojī is proclaimed to be two and a half yavas.
The width of the lower lip is said to be one measure including a barley-corn;
it is protected by seven [units], and the mantra at the root is said to consist of two measures.
The exit should be as long as the parapet wall;
it is described as being thirty-two [units] in length, showing what is invisible and visible.
The upper row of teeth, however, is prescribed as broad and high by three *yavas*;
in the fangs, there is an increase of one *yava*, and they are shaped like buds.
The upper row of teeth should be sixteen, and the lower row likewise;
then the lower row should consist of sixteen teeth, and its width should be one yava.
In the jihvāmūlīya, the height is that of a piśāla, consisting of six mātrās and one mātrā;
the visarga is two mātrās, and the upadhmānīya is three mātrās high, as is desired by the wise.
Beyond that, it should be two barley-corns deep; the ear should be one finger-breadth in measure. (4) The throat should be half a mātrā, struck by the *nivṛt* and *kala*.
The face, resembling the golden moon, was described by the former teachers;
make the neck four mātras long and then one part higher than that.
The neck-ridge is made dark-colored, and the sacrificial post is fashioned with a sharp-edged base;
the top-knot (kakuda) is nine finger-breadths high and adorned with bamboo and other auspicious materials.
The width between the two armpits is proclaimed to be equal to that;
the width of the region for the fragrance is said to be sixteen finger-breadths.
The front part [of the face] should be thirteen and a half finger-breadths, including the waist;
the width of the mandala (the face) is known to be sixteen and a half finger-breadths.
The height of the thighs from the root to the buttocks is considered to be half of that.
Then, from the middle of the nine and eight [fingers], there is half [the distance] to the three seats at the root of Śiva.
His neck is adorned with two lines and is well-rounded and beautiful to behold;
from the line of the *hikā* to the end of his arms, the length measures twenty-seven units.

From that, the width of the knee-cavity is desired to be two hand-fingers; this is proclaimed as the measurement for the *kolaka* and the *kopara*. The length of the palm is prescribed to be exactly six finger-breadths.
The length of the middle finger should be made six finger-breadths.
Then, provided with eight jars and extending outward,
the *hikkāsūtra* should measure one and a half *nandāṅgulas* up to the end of the *ṛkṣas*.
The *hikkāsūtra* and the *tropariskanda* should be made with dimensions decreasing in sequence by one part, one *bhāga*, one *kola*, and one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*),
ending at the tips of the petals.
The width of the base of the arm is one and a half finger-breadths;
the width at the middle of the arm is two finger-breadths plus a barley-corn.
The broadness of the copper [band] at the base of the forearm is six finger-breadths, diminished by one barley-corn and consisting of seven measures.
The width at the middle of the forearm is five measures with one barleycorn;
the width of the wrist is three and a half measures.
The breadth of the palm is said to be six finger-breadths;
it is desired that the span of four mātrās be one finger-length plus one barley-corn.
That same [measurement] is stated as the smallest; six barleycorns constitute the mother-karma [unit].
That which reaches the region of the ring finger is called the lowest finger-breadth.
[Thus ends the chapter on the rules for the number of *tālas* in the *yogaja-pratiṣṭhā*. Homage to the glorious Lord Somanātheśvara, together with the glorious Amṛtāmbā.
Regarding the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (*śūla*):
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme characteristics of the sacrificial pit;
I shall describe its installation for the benefit of all the gods.
The trident, which embodies all the gods, should be made of gold, silver, or copper;
likewise, it may be made of iron if those materials are unavailable—this is the prescribed rule.
At the entrance of the womb and at the hand, one should likewise fashion it with the *tāla* measure;
the middle [type] has its pain concentrated in the womb and has even feet.
Now, the middle part [of the temple] should be known; it shall be described according to its proportion.
The womb-door and the four doors [are formed], or else the elevation is three parts.
The embryo, however, remains within the two limbs of the earth and the being for eight [days];
according to the division into superior and so forth, it is established as three times three.
The triad beginning with the *uttama* is indeed known as the triad beginning with the *madhyama*;
likewise, the triad beginning with the *adhama* is established by the *vayayā-kūrmi*.
That which is equal to a bridge at the opening and devoid of any part of a cavity is called the best *śūla*;
that which is [similarly] described is the middling *śūla*, and the inferior *śūla* is now declared.
A trident lacking five parts is said to be the lowest;
one made of jewels is the best, while one of three cubits is auspicious and middling.
One should know that the minimum [measurement] is two *aratnis*; this is the established rule.
When it is suspended, one should divide thirty degrees and so forth by equal parts.
Having brought together one part until the arising of that auspicious nature, the trident is said to be of two kinds:
both the yogic and the worldly.

The site for the king that is favorable to the sacrificer is called *laukika* (worldly). That which is joined with the measurements of the yogins is called *yautika*. One part of the length of the hall is called the *lāma* of the vessels.
One should perform a single *nāṭikā* there, with an extensive description of the curse.
Having measured the leaf, make it square and even;
then, having opened the leaf-door, place [the vessel] on both sides as well.
Just as one would roll out a circular shape there from the rolled-out clay itself,
one should take the space between those two [circles] and rotate it like a half-moon.
Indeed, the two side-leaves should be made so that they become circular.
And by means of the syllable *pā*, it is joined with whatever [mantras] end in *yā* and *yā*.
One should then form half-buds from the base to the tip of the middle finger in sequence;
the thickness of the leaf-expansion is said to be one part of a ṛṣabha.
The distance between the tip and the base of the two side petals should be half a *tārā*;
the length of the bowl should be divided into nine parts by means of the base alone.
It is declared that the length of a foot [of the wall] is one unit, its width is half of that;
the middle foot is twice as long, and its width is equal to the side foot.
At the base of the petals, one should indeed fashion a circular arrangement;
with various leafy creepers, one should cause the roots of the petals to be fashioned.
One should fashion its *pālikā* from half the width of the leaf;
having divided that silver (*tāra*) into nine parts, one part of space (*vyomāṃśa*) [is used] for the length of the *pālikā*.
With one part, below the lotus, one should fashion a corner like half a leaf for a horse;
likewise, one should arrange a *kravyāda-pālikā* (flesh-eating niche) at half that size. One should then divide the width of the *galī-pālikā* (neck-niche) into ten parts.
Its width at the neck should be one part, and its height should be equal to that.
Having taken half of the measure of the base, the wise one should fashion the ear with a curvature resembling the shape of a half-pot (*pālikārdhaghaṭa*).
With a foot [of measurement] and a *kumbhatāra*, its *ayastaṭikā* would be;
the measure of the *ghaṭavartāṭikā* is [the same] minus one-fourth part.
One part, however, is for the *hikkā*, the *pradaṇḍaka*, and the *tāṭikā*;
those [parts] which have a width of four parts [should be] three parts [in height].
The width of the wooden staff should be [one unit], and the iron staff half of that.
At the base of the staff, there should be a lotus, its width equal to that of the *pālikā*.
It is said that the measurement is half of that; this measurement is divided according to the qualities.
One part is to be known as the fillet (paṭṭikā), while in the remaining parts [is] the lotus.
A wise person should have it made either circular or square;
according to the measurement of the *hirika*, one should fashion a band above the lotus.
In the center of the middle petal, one should draw a lotus facing that [direction].
Thus has the characteristic been described; thereafter, one should perform the consecration.
During the period of the sun's northern course (uttarāyaṇa), in the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa) on an auspicious day,
the wise man should perform the ritual sowing of seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) on the day preceding the day of consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
Sprinkling with water is declared to be the "eye"; one should perform the consecration with products of the cow, accompanied by all musical instruments and endowed with all ornaments.
Having fully adorned the trident, one should perform the circumambulation of the village;
and in the water, one should construct a water-shed provided with four limbs.
Having wrapped it with a new cloth, the trident should remain from the top downwards;
[it should be] knee-deep in water, facing east, with its tip pointing upwards.
Having laid the trident upon a wooden plank with the Sadyojāta mantra,
one should place it for two nights, three nights, or even for a single night in front of the temple; first, one should perform the rites in the pavilion.
Having divided the pavilion into three parts, one should arrange it in the middle of the altar.
One should construct sacrificial pits all around— in the cardinal and intermediate directions— with a height of one cubit and a surface resembling the belly of a mirror.
One should fashion squares in the cardinal directions and a lotus in the corners; between the northeast and the wheel, one should make a principal circle.
In the west or the north, one should arrange a bathing place;
there, one should cause the Brahmins to pronounce the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha), and thereafter feed them.
One should perform the Vāstuhoma sacrifice on ground smeared with cow dung;
one should carry out the rite of circumambulation with fire and again observe the Punyāha ceremony.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) above the altar with eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice,
one should draw a lotus in its center using both rice grains and sesame seeds.
Having scattered parched grain, flowers, and *darbha* grass, especially [in that place],
one should prepare a seat in its center, along with a tiger-skin rug and an offering (*bali*).
Having prepared a garment of golden hue according to the prescribed sequence,
and having emerged from the water, one should place the trident-weapon upon the head after performing the ritual bath.
Having removed the cloth and the trident-weapon, and having performed purification with water from eight jars,
one should bathe [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and consecrate it with pure waters.
Having sprinkled it with the heart-mantra, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Thereafter, the wise one should tie a protective amulet (kautuka) with a thread upon the middle petal;
joined with a golden thread, he should fasten it at the heart with the mantra.
Then, from the head down to the feet, he should wrap [the image] in a new cloth.
One should cause the devotion toward Caṇḍeśvara to be bestowed upon Caṇḍeśāyana.
(Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for the characteristics of the trident in the *Yogaja-pratiṣṭhā-tantra*). Homage to the illustrious Somanātheśvara together with the illustrious Amṛtāmbā.
(The rite of the sacred thread investiture).
Now I shall explain in detail the ritual of offering the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa);
that which is called "pavitra" is designated as "pure."
The gods, dānavas, gandharvas, piśācas, brahmarākṣasas,
all the hosts of niṣṭigyas, and the groups of kṣetrapālas and others;
However, for the sake of the renown of all, perform the Pavitrārohaṇa rite;
one may do so in Āṣāḍha, or in Śrāvaṇa, or even in Bhādrapada.
In Āṣāḍha it is declared to be excellent; in Śrāvaṇa, one should place it as middling;
in Bhādrapada, it is to be known as inferior—thus it is proclaimed according to the three months.

In this manner, the rite should be performed especially on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, or alternatively on the thirteenth day; then follows the offering of fragrant purifiers (gandhapavitraka).
The gold thread is the best, the silver thread is middling, the copper thread is the lowest; however, in the case of a mere fraction [of merit], even cotton thread is acceptable.
Kuśa grass, kāśa grass, and ṛvīṇā grass, gathered together;
likewise, a blindfold for the eyes, and an excellent lotus fiber.
It is said that in the absence of [other materials], one should make it firm with thread;
a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, a maiden, or one who knows the Sūtras [may do so].
One should make the threads fine and avoid using hair-strainers;
having sprinkled it with pure water, one should wash it according to the prescribed rule.
Having decorated the pavilion with cloths and divine ornaments, [one should proceed].
One should decorate the platforms with full water-jars and mirrors.
One should perform the offering of the sprouts there according to the previously mentioned procedure (line 4),
using either twelve, sixteen, or twenty-five [sprouts].
One should place either fifteen, twenty, or one hundred and eight [vessels],
together with the substances for the ritual bath, according to the prescribed procedure.
One should perform the installation of the pitcher (kalaśa) with one's own garment and its lid, provided with gold and jewels, and according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Having first prepared the animal sacrifice, one should then perform [the rite] either in a fire-pit or on a sacrificial mound,
using sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, sesame seeds, and barley.
One should offer all the materials for the fire-oblation in their proper sequence;
specifically, one should offer the sacrificial fuel (*samidh*) and the clarified butter (*ājya*) in order, or one may offer only the clarified butter.
Having taken the sacrificial porridge with the Aghora mantra, the parched grain with the Tatpuruṣa mantra,
the sesame-mixed [grain] with the mantra [of Īśāna], and the mustard seeds with the Kavaca mantra.
Having seized the Āḍakaṃ, the heart, and the finger-measure of Śivā,
as well as the armor, the arrow, and the supreme weapon;
Having offered unbroken grains with the weapon-mantra in due order, and especially [with the specific mantra],
one should perform the fire-oblation thus with the root-mantra for the final full oblation.
One should worship either the *liṅga* or the *kautuka* with a pure bath;
likewise, one should honor the sixteen images with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
One should worship the image in the pavilion or at the water tank in due order; thereafter, one should cause an offering of food (naivedya) to be presented and offer betel-leaf (tāmbūla).
[This is performed] with the recitation of hymns and auspicious readings, and by the sounding of Vedic study.
And with the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, and the like, along with auspicious cries of "Victory! and other such blessings.
One should perform song and dance, and consecrate the sacred vessel;
through the yoga of meditative absorption, one should fashion the eternal jar at night.
Having performed the placement of the purifiers according to the prescribed rule,
one should subsequently perform [the recitation] one hundred and eight times, or fifty, or twenty-five.
They are proclaimed as being of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior.
Twenty-five purifiers (pavitrakas) should be made, with half of them being auspicious (maṅgala).
Measuring with two finger-breadths, or else with the voice and a finger, one should perform the binding there;
one should bind it in sequence with a thread.
Having first performed the binding with saffron, red chalk, collyrium, turmeric, and nutmeg, according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures,
[one obtains] the body, the *haribera*, and the wave named *pūṣpaka*.
The fragrant vessel, however, is a bowl; this is prescribed as their fragrant offering.
Then one should tie a knot according to the number of threads;
one should tie it with a measurement that is appropriate for the phallus.
One should thus diligently prepare a head-ornament (uṣṇīṣa) made of Gaṅgā-vāta-raca;
and [one may drink] from a vessel of gold, silver, or copper.
Endowed with all auspicious marks, vast and most beautiful—
it should be placed in the center of that [mandala] and worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
A new garment should be draped [around it] everywhere; one should place [the vessel] upon that.
One should then arrange the *kūrca* grass-bundle in the pavilion in due order. Having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) in this manner—
In the morning, he should perform purification, ritual sipping of water, bathing, and the twilight worship (*sandhyā-vandana*). Furthermore,
having performed the ritual placement of the deity (*devanyāsa*) according to the procedure on the previous day,
he should offer the thread for the mounting of the Lord (*īśvarārohaṇa-sūtra*) to Caṇḍeśa.
Having placed the water-pots all around and having worshipped them especially,
he should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited by those who proclaim blessings and auspiciousness.
Accompanied by shouts of victory, songs, dances, and the like, together with the loud chanting of the Vedas and other sounds,
[the sound] of kettledrums, hand-drums, tabors, *ekāntala*, *liṅka*, and *ṇṭaka* drums.
With *dhallarīs*, *maddalas*, *kartarīs*, cymbals, and flutes, and with the sounding of conchs and *dundubhī* drums, he should be adorned with all ornaments;
wearing new garments, he should perform the binding of his head-cloth.
He had a golden flower upon his head and wore a sacrificial thread made of gold.
Having circumambulated the Ālaya, which is adorned with all ornaments,
one should then go to the Garbhagṛha and offer the sacred thread (*pavitraka*).

Having performed the worship especially with incense and lamps in due order, one should proceed. Having gone forth from the single house, there is the temple and the encircling of the thread. An offering should then be presented, specifically milk-rice (pāyasa).
There, one should honor the teacher according to one's means;
having fully honored him, the devotees among the practitioners should likewise worship him in due order.
Then, with offerings to his attendants, he should feed the Brāhmaṇas;
he should daily feed the gods on earth (the Brāhmaṇas) according to his means.
But beginning with the Āgama, in the Śivadharma Purāṇa,
one should worship the mouth [of the deity] according to the Purāṇa and then worship the one born from the sacrifice to the gods.
Having installed all the deities under the supervision of others with sacred threads,
he should perform the rite of offering the sacred threads (pavitrārohaṇa) and the cooking of the offerings with his attendants.
He should cause all the people to receive the ear-rings along with the sacred threads for twelve days,
eight days, five days, or even three days.
One should perform the offering of the *pavitra* there at the proper time;
having placed the *pavitraka* in its position, one should properly join it at the conclusion of the worship.
Then, one should provide a mount together with a rider, fully adorned with all ornaments;
taking the previously consecrated [image], one should offer it to Caṇḍeśa. There, one should perform the ceremonial bath and worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Afterwards, having honored the ascetic, one should attend to him with clothing.
One should cause the yogis to receive the loincloth, the upper garment, and the full set of limbs;
the forest-dwelling initiation, the purificatory rites, and the circumambulation.
One should avoid needlework and other such tasks during these nights and days.
One should avoid the maṇḍala [in the first case], or it may be entwined by a creeper;
likewise, it may be a lotus maṇḍala or even a half-moon.
In the first part of the night, they should worship the mental aspect of the Ācārya;
there, at the time when the worship is concluded, one should worship the Maṇḍala.
Having adorned the pavilion, one should prepare all the ritual substances:
a mirror, a fly-whisk, and painted palm-leaf fans;
then the application of hair, wood, and the animation of nails, hair, and so forth.
A garment, an ornament, a bowl, the application of ashes, and a water-pot.
A wrist-band, a girdle, a support, and a loincloth;
and for the application of collyrium, a vessel and two applicator-sticks.
A yoga-band, a water-strainer, or a black antelope skin made of muñja grass;
a conch-shell vessel, [an ornament] of the five metals, and the eight auspicious weapons.
One should place the tortoise-posture for all [deities] and construct a pavilion;
[place] a black deer and an axe, with an alms-bowl positioned below.
The divine weapon, the divine fragrance, the sun, the moon, and fire;
the Gaṅgā, the armlet, and the garland—these also belong to the rite of the eight nāgas.
The Rudramālā, the Śiromālā, and the Uṣṇīṣamāyā;
the Lalāṭamālā, the Karṇamālā, and the Karṇanālabandhakā.
From the heart center to the hanging garland, make the abode of intoxication;
there are the rosary of recitation, the arm-garland, and various other garlands for the hands and arms.
Taking the vessel, one should place it before the maṇḍala;
in this very same sequence, one should likewise set out the ritual substances.
One should worship that [deity] at the conclusion of the Pavitrārohaṇa rite;
the mortal who performs it in this manner shall attain a meritorious state.
The preliminary rite should be performed according to the ritual requirements for the purification of the limbs during the Pavitrāroha;
likewise, the scripture associated with the Goddess is the scripture of the Pavitrārohaṇa.

[Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for the investiture of the sacred thread (*pavitrārohaṇa*) in the *Yogaja-pratiṣṭhā-tantra*. Homage be to the venerable Somanātheśvara, together with the venerable Amṛtāmbā! Homage!
May there be the glance of grace from the venerable Manonukūleśvara together with the venerable Śītaleśvarī. (f.
31a) Regarding the ritual procedure for the mandala: now I shall speak specifically; the form of the mandala is described.
The pavilion is divided into four parts, and one part is for the altar (vedikā).
One should draw a mandala in the center with a height of one palm-tree span, resembling the surface of a mirror, and measuring five palm-trees in extent.
Having drawn a grid of eight times eight squares,
