one should delineate four central compartments in the form of a lotus pedestal, colored white, red, and black.
Having drawn yellow and dark lotuses for all [the deities],
the wise one should arrange a white path outside the lotus pedestal.
Likewise, one should arrange four sacrificial fires: the Rakta, the Vidhi which is reddish-black, the Kṛṣṇaka, and the Pīta which is likewise the Nyāya.
One should make the door-arch (dvārārdhamāraka); this is called the karṇovakarṇa.
One should make the cheek-projections (kapolakapolaka) outside the Brahma-sthāna.
The *vṛkti* should be three finger-breadths; the half-moon (*ardhacandraka*) is three finger-breadths;
the lotus (*padma*) is likewise three finger-breadths; and the svastika is three finger-breadths.

The Śrīvatsa, measuring three finger-breadths and four square units in size, should be placed; it may be white, red, yellow, black, or dark green. A footprint distributed on all sides is desired for the Sarvatobhadra design.
With rice flour one makes the white [mark], and with red lac the red [mark].
Haridrā is yellow; kṛṣṇa and śyāma constitute the pentad.
Dagdhaliḍā is black; kṛṣṇa is the word, the counter-form, and the action.
Having drawn the mandala in all [directions] according to the sequence and the enclosure,
listen now to the Sarvatobhadra [mandala] arising from the entwining of creepers:
having made it with sixty-four squares, there is a four-square lotus in the center.
One should especially draw eight petals in five colors.
One should fashion a lotus four units in width, nourishing it with the *kauśika* part;
one should make the pericarp with the *vyoma* part, and the filaments with the *pakṣa* portion.
The remaining petals, however, should extend to the measure of half a karṇikā;
outside the lotus, within half a portion, it should be fashioned in white color.
It has four gates equal in measure to the main structure, supported by beautiful archways;
it possesses many pinnacles equal to that [main structure], with secondary ornaments matching the beauty of the primary ones.
In the four directions starting from Īśāna, red, reddish-brown, white,
and black powder is prescribed, especially from a skull.
From Indra to Soma (the sixth line), one should arrange the liṅgas in the four directions;
having made seven steps for the liṅga, there should be four steps for the outer pedestal.
The three-footed Liṅga is "udhva" (upward-facing), with the faces of Puruṣa and the others;
it is fashioned as a four-faced Liṅga, extending from Indra to Soma in the four directions.
From Indra to Soma, there shall be twenty-eight positions;
the wise one should arrange them according to their respective numbers in the half-liṅga design.
One should likewise fashion them as yellow, black, white, and blue.
One should fill each corner up to the dative case-ending in reverse order.
Thus, perform the "Arising from the Embrace of the Creeper" (latāliṅgotbhava) with the mind of the Preceptor.
I shall now describe the "Arising from the Mind of the Preceptor" (ācāryamanobhava); listen with a one-pointed mind.
Having made the ground level, resembling the surface of a mirror,
one should [draw] a thread with its tip pointing east and likewise with its tip pointing north.
In the center, there is a nine-square lotus, endowed with eight petals and filaments.
A wise man should cause a temple to be constructed with nine divisions in the four directions.
Equipped with the six groups of deities and adorned with the [deities] beginning with Nāsikya,
one should construct the temple as before, having divided it into eight equal parts.
It should have two bands or a foot-band around the base, with the linga clearly marked;
it should be joined to the pedestal and consist of three parts divided according to the group of squares.
The Koṇesvastika is said to be distinguished by nine divisions;
it has five lines of powder and five openings, specifically for the Puruṣa and others. One should construct the temple with a face like that [of the deity] and arrange it according to the sequence.
One should arrange the eight powers, Vāmā and the others, around the periphery.
One should perform the worship in sequence by means of the path of the five obstructions;
one should draw a mandala all around with three hundred lines, exceeding the universe.
One should fashion a single, non-perverted [image] with five faces.
A plantain fruit, an ātrā fruit, breast-milk, and sugar—[these are the materials].
One should worship the mandala with perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
One should fashion [the image] weighing one niṣka, or half of that, or even half of that again.
One should place a flower-offering upon the pavilion;
[one should give] at least one hundred niṣkas, or as much as one can obtain, like a mountain.
In the eastern direction from the mandala, a golden mountain is desired;
in the south, a silver one and so forth;
in the southwest (rākṣasa), having placed jewels, one should place a copper mountain and the like in the west.
Having established the Mukta mountain in the direction of Varuṇa (the west), [he placed] the Vāyu and Lavaṇa mountains.
Soma and mustard seeds and so forth are for Śiva; sesame seeds and so forth are for Śāṅkara.
In this manner, all [the substances] are released, either individually or by the measure of a bhāra.
One should perform the rite according to what is available and fashion a mountain;
the wise practitioner should offer oblations with the five Brahmans, the six limbs, and the Jayā-mantras.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth by means of his own name,
the knower of mantras should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with rice grains in due order on the northern part of the mandala.
In the center of that, the wise one should prepare a bed with red cloth;
then, having performed the binding of the eyes, he should wrap [the disciple] in a new garment.
One should tie the protective amulet there and perform the binding of the weapons;
a night-homa must be performed, and one should offer oblations to all the gods.
"Make a double-layered covering for the God of Gods.
At the clear dawn, one should release the blindfold there.
Having placed a golden flower upon it, one should cause his name to be bestowed."
One should cause the deity to be bathed with fifty or twenty-five [verses].
Or one may offer a hundred and eight oblations to the God of gods;
furthermore, one should cause a golden auspicious thread and a new garment to be given.
Having offered abundant oblations, one should propitiate the God of gods;
having worshipped all the deities, one should cause them to behold the mandala.
One should cause all the implements of the sacrifice to be given to the preceptor;
one should perform an ablution with ghee and milk, and bathe him with a coconut.
One should offer the deity together with Umā and Skanda a large quantity of betel-leaf mixed with poison;
there, one should have the devotees and attendants present it.
One should worship the devotees there according to one's ability with attendants;
one should feed the Brahmins there and provide them with gifts according to one's means.
One should worship the teacher there and observe the prescribed conduct until death;
having received the instruction of the Śiva-mantra, one should then worship the teacher.
If the wise teacher should pass away first, the disciple should enter his own home.
[Thus ends the chapter on the ritual procedure for the mandala in the Yogaja-pratiṣṭhā-tantra].

May there be the compassionate glance of the grace of the venerable Lord Somanātheśvara, together with the venerable Amṛtāmbā. With the assistance of the venerable Manonukūleśvara, together with the venerable Śitalāmbā, [follows] the ritual for the ripening of the fruit.
Now, therefore, I shall duly explain the procedure for the ripening of fruits;
having seen the Lord of the Mountain Peak from afar, a man becomes a master of the sacred syllable Om (Praṇaveśvara).
One who strides from step to step while circumambulating the abode of Śiva is liberated from all sins and becomes free from delusion.
That affliction, however, shall become auspicious through Māyā, which destroys all evil;
likewise, one who has touched the water [of initiation] shall be well-liberated in the world of mortals.
Just as a person who performs a circumambulation during a festival or at the time of an offering obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice for every step,
so too does one who honors the world by performing the proper rites.

One should offer water-borne flowers or land-grown flowers dedicated to the Lord. Having adorned the garden of the God of gods with various kinds of flowers, that man enjoys manifold pleasures on earth.
Thus, the illustrious Sathanavān was highly honored in this world;
he spent ten thousand and a hundred thousand years at the feet of the Vedapāraka, who was rich in yoga.
One should bathe the presiding deity with cow’s horn using milk,
along with the five products of a tawny cow (*kapilā-pañcagavya*) mixed with the water of the *kulavāri* [family vessel].

One should bathe the Lord of the gods of gods; the fruit is equal to the gift of ten million [coins]. A person who performs the ninefold bathing with perfect devotion enjoys pleasures and is glorified in the world of Śiva.
In the ninth path, however, the experience of the vital points (marmas) occurs in nine ways.
Having divided the oblation into nine parts, that fruit is for Guru and Īśvara. The incense-stick which is offered first remains for Agni and Nirṛti.
One should cause garments, ornaments, and so forth to be offered to the God of gods—
[the shrine] filled with various cloths and various ornaments.
Having been honored here in this world, he especially possesses power;
even upon ground the size of a cow's ear, he is of an unshakable nature, like Umā’s consort.
Even the lord of villages is especially honored here;
moreover, one becomes a single-stemmed *praśnī* tree in the vicinity of the God of Gods.
One should cause the lamp of the God of gods to be offered once at the proper time;
for in all worlds, he is like a lamp because of his nature as the source of all trees.
One who undertakes [the rite] at its commencement with Śiva in mind shall again partake of heaven;
furthermore, the fruit that is proclaimed for all types of gifts shall be obtained through this sacrifice.
Therefore, one shall obtain this great fruit in the form of an extraordinary heaven;
by means of its water, which is both perishable and imperishable, one will be nourished for seven births.
Whether constructing [shrines] from brick, stone, or iron,
or even from gold, a man who performs such deeds is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Established by means of a pure celestial vehicle according to the path of ritual procedure,
one attains the world of Śiva while being honored for one's virtuous conduct.
After a Śivaliṅga has been established, one shall attain the fruit of union (sāyujya). Whatever material was used to install the liṅga, from that very material it will arise [for the worshiper].
When the Śiva-sacrifice is completed, one should perform whatever rites have been prescribed.
And likewise, he [learned] the names of twenty-one generations of his own lineage.
They desire ten previous births from beyond the tenth [birth] after sitting;
that is held to be their station in the world for those who have not yet brought forth offspring.
Those [merits] of those who desire to hear [the scriptures] are attained through sons, brothers, and wives;
indeed, by him alone is the world of Śiva reached, which is superior to all other worlds of the gods.
Then, having offered extensive oblations when the dissolution has arrived,
and having attained the yoga of knowledge, one is liberated from the body.

One should construct enclosures and pavilions as prescribed; by doing so, one attains heaven. By diligently constructing ponds, wells, and tanks dedicated to the deities, one becomes possessed of great wealth and, at the end of that life, shall attain Śiva.
In that case as well, for the majority of them, there is no doubt that they will attain heaven.
Having understood the state of one seated upon a seat, one should worship Śiva;
[one attains] sālokya, sāmīpya, and indeed sārūpya.
Sāyujya is indeed fourfold: the highest, the middle, the lowest, and the intermediate.
The four pillars have Dharma, Jñāna, and so forth as their presiding deities.
On the outside, the twelfth [section] belongs to the suns; it has the twelve Ādityas as its deities.
Of the outer [pillars], there are twenty pillars, dedicated to the Vasus and the two Aśvins.
And having wrapped Vidyeśvara and Viśvau— the deities who support the universe—
with garlands of darbha grass and adorned them with flower garlands;
Having encircled the false archway (tāṭaṅka), it was also wound around the pillars;
it was adorned with white cloths fastened above and decorated with eye-covers (netrapaṭa).
A coconut fruit adorned with flowers and strings of pearls,
and an aśvattha tree embellished with red leaves and cakes.
Provided with perfumes and flowers, and adorned with incense and lamps,
one should smear the ground with cow dung and sprinkle it with water.
Just as the preliminary rite was previously performed with the offering of the sprouts, so too was the pavilion prepared beforehand; now hear from me the time for the dance.
In the daily bath, everything up to the end of the worship is performed in the same manner;
this is likewise true for the milk bath, the ghee bath, the honey bath, or even the water bath.
On any other auspicious day as well, one should perform his dance; before the first dance, offer a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the women.
Likewise, for the Gandharva who is the first among the breakers of the earth.
Nṛttakomardala and likewise Gāyakovaṃśaka.
Indeed, he bestows the initiation of Śiva upon the women of Rudra and Māraka;
[he initiates one] endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament.
One should commence the pure dance (śuddhanṛtta) when endowed with these characteristics;
[it should not be performed by one] lacking limbs, nor by one who is nasalized, nor by a child, nor likewise by an old man.
One who has diseased or deformed limbs, as well as those afflicted by consumption, leprosy, and the like, should be avoided;
likewise, one should avoid atheists and those of perverse conduct.
One should avoid a woman endowed with such characteristics as these;
she should be possessed of fingers of equal length and provided with hands of moderate size.
Accompanied by the *ahidyāya* [instrument], joined with palm-clapping (*tālavanta*),
endowed with all ornaments, it is pure dance (*śuddhanṛtta*) set to song.
That which is endowed with these characteristics is declared to be Gāndharva;
thus has the fault of dancing on the bank of a river been proclaimed.
For the sake of neutralizing those defects, there is a bath consisting of twenty-five [substances];
one should worship either the *liṅga* or the *kautuka* with perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
Prior to that, one should perform pure dances and other rites during the night for the consecration (*adhivāsana*).
In the northern part of the pavilion, prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) covered with rice.
One should prepare a bed there and arrange it so that it is free from birth;
in its center, one should place the wives of Rudra, clad in garments of silk.
Having tied the protective thread (kautuka), one should cause [the image] to lie down and then thread it with a golden string;
likewise, there should be a dancer, a masseur, a singer, and a lute-player.
One should consecrate the musical instruments and the drum during the night;
there, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with eight droṇas of śāli rice.
With half that amount of rice and with half that again of sesame seeds,
one should place nine jars endowed with the nine Śaktis.
Together with a water-pot (kūrca), a lid, and fresh sprouts along with cloths,
one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and the like, accompanied by incense and lamps.
Having risen at dawn and performed purification and sipping of water (ācamana),
one should specifically perform a bath accompanied by the cleansing of the teeth;
then, having established [the image] with nine pitchers while recollecting the initiation mantra (dīkṣā-mantra).
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should present [the image] together with garments and ornaments.
One should place a flower upon the head with the heart-mantra;
having cast the flower into the hand, one should likewise observe where the flower falls.
One should daily recite that name of Rudra’s consort in the proper sequence;
thereafter, one should perform a circumambulation and cause her to enter the temple. Having paid obeisance to Vighneśa, one should offer fruit and flowers.
One should likewise worship Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, and the goddess Śrī.
Having offered fragrant flowers and oblations, one should cause betel-leaf to be presented;
at midday, however, one should offer milk-rice as excellent food for the wives of Rudra.
Then, entering the pavilion amidst the various women,
one should worship the Vāstu deities, beginning with Īśāna.
In the evening, one should offer the bali-oblation to the deities of the pavilion;
in the center of that pavilion, prepare either a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or a layer of sesame seeds.
Having placed that sound in the midst [of them], one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
then, having covered it with a new, unwashed cloth, one should cause sacrificial food (haviṣya) to be offered.
Having worshipped Nandikeśvara, one should honor him with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
first, the purification of oneself, and second, the cleansing of the hands.
The third is called Vaṃśatāla, declared to be the group of Oṃkāras;
the fourth is Nagaśuddhi, and the fifth is Muravādya.
The sixth is joined with instrumental music; the seventh is the scattering of flowers;
the eighth is the binding of the wrist; one should contemplate the ninth as (...
[the tenth is] the completion of the dance—these are the characteristics of the dance.
The preceptor sat comfortably on the right side of the god.
In the northern region of the god, the two who were reciting the Ṛgveda sat comfortably;
in the western part of the god, the attendant was well-established.
The dancer and the drummer are stationed to the south,
while the singer and the flute-player are stationed to the north.
On both sides stood the wives of Rudra,
and in the eastern direction were stationed the great sounds of the mṛdaṅga drums and other instruments.
Other devotees also stood outside that [enclosure];
having performed the lustration ceremony (nirājana) as before with hymns and auspicious recitations, they remained there.
There, one should honor the teacher with garments, gold, and finger-rings;
one should also cause a tambourine, a musical instrument, a pair [of shoes], and a garment to be given to him.
One should also offer betel leaf to these people of other castes;
[one should provide] music arising from song and instrumental performance, as well as instrumental music produced with rhythmic clapping.
"Tālanṛktasamutbhavam" means "arisen from rhythmic timing and dance. These are known as the origins; thus, the dance performed upon the stage is called *raṅgevartam*.
One should contemplate the hands and the eyes as the final determination, resting upon the *bhāvapāta* and *tāla*;
[one should likewise contemplate] the head, hands, waist, face, the golden [ornaments], and the joined sides.
The characteristics of dance consist of the coordination of major and minor limbs;
the characteristics of dance consist of being joined with rhythm (*laya*) and tempo (*tāla*).
One should perform a beautiful dance through the union of *laya* and *tāla*.
In the absence of song, there is no rain; in the absence of instrumental music, there is the destruction of fuel.
If the *nṛta* (dance) is lacking, there is poverty; if the *tāla* (rhythm) is lacking, it is terrifying.
With the sounds of the *bindu*, *vāda*, vowels, and consonants, [the sound] reaches the navel region.
(The six *ṛṣabha*, *ṛṣabha*, and *gāndhāra* [notes], with *madhyama* as the presiding deity.)
The heart, the form, the throat, the teeth, and the tongue;
between the white and the red [is] Śiva, who arises from the Bindu and the Nāda.
In its center is the state of *praṇa*, the form of the *bindu*, which is higher than the highest;
it is said to be the flow of *māyā* within the seven vowels— this is the sequence of the ritual in the *sakala* [state].
The Ṛṣabha, Gāndhāra, Madhyama, Pañcama, and Daivata notes,
as well as Niṣāda and Niṣkala, constitute the "with-sound" (sasvara) state of the "with-parts" (sakala) scale.
The manifest (sakala) must be the support and the object of worship for the partless (niṣkala);
the manifest would be of the nature of power (śakti), while the partless is of the nature of the individual soul (jīva).
The breath, which is the support of the tone, should become equal to the vital air;
the air, having entered the lotus-stalk, is joined with the force of the birth-pain.
As is space, so is wind; its sound should have that same measure.
They say the syllable *sa* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and likewise the syllable *ra* is fire.
Through the conjunction of these two syllables, the tone of the vowel is perceived.
The sixteen-syllable mantra beginning with 'a' and ending with the visarga, which is victorious.

The beginning of the consonant, its luster, and its expansion as well as its non-origination; likewise, the yellow, the *aikha*, the *kāra*, and the graceful (*lalita*)—thus one should grasp their unity.
Time is said to be the fourth *mardala*, consisting of the union of the three groups of seven notes;
having formed a representation of the syllables through twenty-one melodic modulations (*mūrchanās*).
One should [know] the Ghaṇṭāgāni, the Nigāyaka, the Sāmin, the Śrutikāra, and that which is adorned with the seven notes (*saptasvara*) existing in Saugrāma and joined with the pure *Ṣāḍava*;
these are the characteristics by which one should specifically distinguish among the various types of flutes (*vaṃśaka*).
In the eighth [measure], there are eight *guru*s first, sixteen *laghu*s in the middle;
thus, the wise one should know that thirty-two *bundu*s are to be performed.
Dhruvakā, Apasarpaṇī, Tiṣyabandhā, Sañjanā—
these are the names by which she is known— and Kavacapatitā is indeed the eighth.
For one who practices that [raga], there are these six types of rāgas: Pañcamī, Indalā, Mālakauśika, Gāndhāra, and Mayākumbha.
The *utsvā* (or *utsavā*) moving at the feet, the *mācaryā*, the *gacārikā*,
and the *mahācāri*— these are the four types of *tāla* for the fourth [measure].
The *dhruva-ākṣipti-laya*, the *vikṣipta*, and the *kṣipta*;
the *āveṣṭita*, the *dveṣṭita*, and likewise the *udveṣṭita*;
the *samapāda*, the *daṇḍapāta*, and the *supuṣpāñjali*.
And likewise bracelets and earrings made of refined gold.
The *sāttvika* dance, joined with [divine] vision, is prescribed for pure performance.
It is also [employed] by *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, *asuras*, hosts of *ogas*, and *rākṣasas*.
O dancing-eyed one, the sound of many husbands reaches your ears; likewise, the terrifying sound of "huṃ" and the terrifying song reach your ears, and together they come from outside.
For this indeed brings peace to the world, increases the king and his kingdom,
and is said to ensure stability, growth, and an abundance of wealth and grain.
Then, for the sake of the lotus-born one, they beheld him who has the luster of a curved bow, who wears a crown of tawny matted locks,
who is yellow, who is the syllable *gaṃ*, and who is the mere end of destruction.
O God of the thirteenth day, whose feet are worshipped by the hosts of Asuras, grant us refuge in the morning;
[grant] the refuge of all worlds.
[Grant] the destruction [of obstacles], the feet of the Lord of Physicians, absorbed in dance.
Seated upon a white bull, wearing white garments, and possessing a white Ganges;
O you whose matted locks are washed by the ocean, who have made the white moon your upper garment,
who possess a white skull-staff, and who are the refuge of the moon-bearer— salutations to you!
And having led [the child] into the pavilion especially before the Lord,
one should place the young child— who has washed his hands— upon the square-shaped body-couch within that pavilion.
Puṣpāñjali, accompanied by the Sudrā (Niroga) and the Sahasrā, is endowed with the dance of Nṛttākṣipti.

O Four-faced One, may there be the attainment of success through this single [hymn] consisting of verses measured by the size of bees, bumblebees, birds, and Brahmins, which is like a handful of water offered with great devotion to the Great Ox.
When the wrists are contracted and free from circular rotation,
and the movement is performed with instruments either on the ground or in the air, it becomes the *kamala* (lotus) *vartanā*.
Overpowered by the song-like humming of bees intoxicated by honey, my mind has become bewildered in this forest that possesses the fragrance of celestial groves;
it enters the woods like a female elephant entering through the forest paths.
Līlā, playful with her mind, moved about with compassion;
she, whose face was like the orb of the moon, entered slowly with steady steps, her lotus-like breasts swaying gently in the auspicious breeze.

May he who sits upon the lotus throne accept this handful of flowers, accompanied by the sweet humming of swarms of bees intoxicated by various fragrances and filled with *mandāra* blossoms, and by glances adorned with various graceful gestures of the hands.
Victory to Gaṅgādhara! Victory to the bearer of the khaṭvāṅga! Victory to the one who is beyond the senses!
Victory to the wearer of the garland of human skulls! Victory to the destroyer of Tripura! (6th line) Victory to him whose feet are worshipped by the entire world of existence! Victory!
O white one, conqueror of the hosts of excellent bulls, destroyer of the multitude of diseases,
you who traverse the feet of the Lord of Physicians, the divine healer!
O you who dwell in the lotus-mansion of the pure lotus-mine of Gāndhāra;
O you who are beloved by the Lotus-Seated One; O you whose dark and light eyes are worshipped by the lotuses!

O Goddess Sarasvatī, who delights in song and instrumental music, who is the abode of virtues and vices, who is saluted by the gods, who is praised by Namī, and who is likewise honored by Karaṇa— you who possess excellent qualities!
At the feet of Jayagaṇapati, who is accompanied by his consort, beneath a dense canopy of clouds,
amidst a blazing multitude of celestial nymphs, and upon a lotus-seat as vast as the earth, he is seen in the midst of the playful dance of worldly existence.

When the wind and moon have been swallowed by the serpent-like mountain, and the sound of the mountain-nymphs' songs has dissolved into the cries of the cuckoos from the hollows, the bees enter as if into a supreme state of intoxication—cast forth by their own satiety. *Triptākṣiptaḥ* (The cast-off by satiety).

Delighted by the song of the *madhavi* flowers and the humming of the swarms of bees, and charmed by the melodies of the *kinnaras*, the immortal one enters the mountain peak—the abode of the lord of elephants—which is slow-moving like Mount Mandara. (Dhravas)

Seated upon his lotus throne, may he accept this handful of flowers, offered with various wonderful gestures and glances by the *puṇṇāga*, sandalwood trees, lotuses, creepers, intoxicated bees, *tāla*, *yogā*, *vakula*, *utpala*, and *karṇikāra* trees. *Puṣpāñjaliḥ* (The Handful of Flowers)

[He who is] adorned with a garland of heads and carrying a skull-bowl, who brings about the destruction of half-Kāma, and possesses a terrifying form—homage to him, the one who has gone forth! [This is] the purity of the five aggregates.
The god, bearing a divine skull-bowl and a trident, with a skeleton for his ornament,
the moon as his crest-jewel, wearing a garland of human heads, and possessing the terrifying Vāsukī as a serpent-necklace with its jewel-encrusted hoods.
O Lord of the Form Realm, one-eyed, like a teacher to the gods and deities of the three worlds—homage be to you!
You who cause the entry [into the path], who produce the guru-like *añjana* and *bhasma*, and who bring about the destruction of the city of the sense objects within the womb.

Drawn by the dance, he who brings about the destruction of that [dance] through his own method, the bearer of the fire-stick for the extinction of death—bow down to Keśava, the remover of the world’s distress.
Having seen Govardhana, which had been lifted by the Lord of the Malasuras to protect the people,
and having beheld the white ash on His own hand, I bow my head to the Lord of the three worlds, the Master of the senses.

May he who sits upon the lotus throne accept this handful of flowers with glances that circle in the yoga of vision, like the petals of a lotus in a pond where intoxicated bees hover around the pericarp. *The Handful of Flowers* (Puṣpāñjali).

The Fish, the Tortoise, and the Boar; Narasiṃha with his frowning brow and crown; the slayer of Kaṃsa; the destroyer of the gods and demons; the one who took away the wealth of the gods; the one who struck down Tripura; the one who seized the fire from the ocean-abode; the divine one; the arrival of the charioteer; the one who makes the belly of Śakra [empty]; the destroyer of Haja; the supreme victory of Viṣṇu of supreme bliss; the supreme one; the maker of the name of Nṛsiṃha.
Homage to the one who holds the wealth of the half-moon, who is adorned with divine elephants and the lord of serpents;
homage to the one accompanied by the goddesses of the directions; homage to the one surrounded by a multitude of various trees bowed down by the finest flowers.
As if entering a bridegroom’s chamber, the forest— sweet with the sound of wandering songs and gently stirred by the wind—
was filled with the joy of bees and the humming of swarms;
it was a grove of very young trees where the Yavanas had grown lax.
When the elephant-king entered the Alaka grove, he ascended into the sky upon his feet, which were adorned with the rays of his tusks. (2nd line) [This was done] by those who were held [in awe].
One should offer flowers and other items of exquisite fragrance upon the sacrificial grass spread out,
accompanied by the Gāyatrī, Vṛkṣakula, Kati, Vandana, and other mantras.
May he who dwells upon the lotus throne, with his hands there offering full and perfect glances, accept from me this handful of flowers. (The Handful of Flowers)
O Lord of Serpents, whose hand bears the excellent Madhu-flower, who has mounted the supreme bull;
O Lion among men, whose garment is the hide of a deer, adorned with a crown of matted locks graced by the crescent moon;

O Kauśika, pure one; O Vāsudeva, whose feet are served by the Lord of the gods; O Goddess, whose face is like a pair of young brides; constant teacher of all beings—[I take refuge in] you, the one who brings forth transcendence.
In the forest, the bees, fearing the color of his leaf-like [garment], were driven away by the fragrance of his excellent scent;
the elephant, with its trunk raised high as if to strike with its tusks, entered the jewel-like [forest] with its trunk extended. This is the *nṛttakṣipti* (the casting-off dance).
O Goddess whose feet are worshipped by the crowns of the gods, including Kamala and Sura; whose pair of lotus-feet is served by sages, Siddhas, and deities;

whose feet are honored throughout the three worlds; who illuminates the dull Veda through the light of the Siddhānta; and who is adorned with bracelets refined by the movements of Hara—[I bow to you].
Salutations to the signs of the Yoginīs, which are held by the [Yogins] with various gestures such as the lotus and the *pārijāta*;
they form a divine garland through the embrace of the *brahma-pariphaṅga* and the *jareta-sūkta*, and by the movements of hands and the casting of glances.
May the one seated upon the lotus throne accept my handful of flowers. (Handful of Flowers)
The Fish, Tortoise, Boar, and Narasimha [incarnations], the frown upon his brow, the crown,
the destruction of the great Asuras and gods, the bestowing of gifts, the slaying of Tripura, and the hurling [of the mountain].
The water, the house, the fire, the divine Śākara, the milk, the ageless, the supreme,
the one who gladdens the supreme, the victorious, the remover of sin, the cause of renunciation, and the arrival of the goal— [these are the names].
Homage to the bearer of the crescent moon, who has half his body destroyed; homage to the one whose food is the divine moon;
homage to the one adorned with ornaments made by the *nāgas*; homage to the one accompanied by the goddess Umā; homage to those who enter [the path].
The song of the one who has made his abode upon the highest peak of the mountain is heard, as he plays the lute with half-illusion.
Bow down to Keśava, the remover of sins, the giver of boons, the elephant among men. (7th line) ……raḥ. This is the *nṛttākṣipti* [dance-introduction].
When the lord of the beasts was free from impurity, when the excellent trees were blossoming and their leaves had fallen,
when the *vakula* trees were fragrant with the scent of ripened flowers, and when the lordly elephant entered, his wrinkles had vanished.

May he who dwells upon the lotus-throne accept this handful of flowers, offered by those whose fame has spread far and wide, who are adorned with garlands and the splendor of their worshipped feet, and who cast glances like blossoming lotuses from within the circles formed by their clasped hands.
The single form of the One, which possesses many hands and feet, with jewels situated on its palms and ears as its whorls,
and whose feet are honored by the multitude of deer and other beings— may that Lord, who is the essence of the sacrifice, grant us the joy of abundant prosperity.

I bow to this one who is the form of Śiva, the casket containing the entire lineage of sages, the bestower of boons upon the excellent people of Cindabena, the departure [from worldly existence], and the one mounted upon fragrance.

Having performed the rites of emergence and entry, and having initiated the transformation, for one who is gladdened by the yoga of the flow [of breath], there is the liberation from the body through the great practice of the essence of the water of delight, which is the very nature of the enemy of the senses, attained through the moon-like jewel of desire.
[Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for the ripening of results in the *Pratiṣṭhātantra* belonging to the *Yaugaja* tradition.]
Salutations to the illustrious Lord Somanātheśvara, accompanied by the illustrious Amṛtāmbā.
Salutations to the glorious Manonmanakūleśvara, together with the glorious Śītalāmbā, residing in the illustrious city of Mahisāra.
Salutations to the illustrious Mahāsarasvatī. Salutations to the illustrious Guru Kumāra. Homage be to him! (f.
42a) I shall now declare the glorious five-syllabled [mantra]; listen with a one-pointed mind.
The letter *na*, the five *makāras*, the letter *śi*, the letter *va*, and the letter *ya* joined with the five; preceded by the *praṇava*, this is the six-syllable [mantra].
The fifth of the fourth group of five, and the fifth of the fifth group of five.
The sixth consists of five times five, endowed with the seed-syllable of Māyā.
The fourth syllable of the seventh [mantra], joined with the second syllable and conjoined with the seed-syllable of Yama (preceded by the *praṇava*), is known as the Śiva-mantra.
The letter *na* is said to be the Ṛgveda; the letter *a* is the Yajurveda;
the letter *śi* is the Sāmaveda; and the letter *va* is the Atharvaveda.

The syllable *ya* is proclaimed as belonging to the entire body; it consists of five syllables, beginning with *na* and ending with *ya*, extending from Brahmā to Sadāśiva. It possesses the *gaītamā* measure, and its seers are Viśvāmitra and Aṅgiras.
And likewise, he honored the sage Bhāradvāja, whose name begins with the letter 'na'.
From *sadyojāta* up to the fifth face, there should be the letters beginning with *na*;
having placed the letter *ma* on the crown and the letter *va* on the forehead.
One should place the syllable *śi* at the region of the ears and the syllable *ma* at the heart;
one should place the syllable *na* at the region of the navel, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in due order.
The creation [of the elements] beginning with the head has been described; one should perform the dissolution [nyāsa] beginning from the feet.
The creation-nyāsa is declared to extend from the little toe to the thumb.
The withdrawal-nyāsa is said to begin from the little finger and end at the thumb.
The placement of the ring finger in the middle is declared to be the nyāsa of stability.
[Thus ends the chapter on the ritual of the five syllables in the Yogaja-pratiṣṭhā-tantra.]
Salutation to the glorious Lord Somanātheśvara, accompanied by the glorious Amṛtāmbā.
Now I shall explain the determination of dissolution (*vibhava-niścaya*) in detail; listen to the determination of dissolution.
It is said that there are two types of sequence: the one with nectar (*sāmṛta*) and the one that takes away (*hāraka*).

The consumption [of offerings] by Śiva has now been declared; however, for the attendants, it is a source of seizure. One who is incapable should make it nectar (amṛta), while one who is capable should make it a source of seizure.
Worship as prescribed by the scriptures shall belong to Śaṅkara.
Having selected one hundred and eight Ādiśaivas who are endowed with austerity and possess the characteristics previously described, [he should perform the rite].
It is recorded as being three, five hundred, or even seven, eight, or nine;
beginning with three and ending with ten powers, according to the extent of one's capacity.
The Guru should cause those belonging to the Śaiva tradition, such as the Hāṭvās, to plant a complete body [of trees];
he should give water, land, gold, grain, and this very earth.
There shall be that same number of *śilākārins*, that same number of ascetics (*tapasvin*),
that same number of musicians (*vādyaka*), and that same number of *āṇikas*.
There were that same number of potters, that same number of flower-keepers,
that same number of temple-maidens, and that same number of washermen.
Likewise, one should provide food according to their means for the friends of that [king], as well as for carpenters, cowherds,
and those who subsist by other crafts.
To the extent of one's strength and resources, one should cause the Dharma to be bestowed;
likewise, according to one's ability, one should provide half of the sacrificial oblation as well as worship and enjoyments.
Thus, that enjoyment is for the sake of lamps; likewise, that enjoyment is for the sake of incense;
likewise, that enjoyment is for the sake of flowers; and that enjoyment is also for the sake of bathing.
The asterism Kṛttikā is for festivals, for fortune, for the enjoyment of flowers,
for the purpose of expiation, and for celestial enjoyment.
Furthermore, there are three types of enjoyment:
enjoyment beyond what is prescribed, enjoyment consisting of the sacrifice to the gods, and enjoyment consisting of the study of the Vedas.
The enjoyment of the Brahma-feast and the enjoyment of the special sacrificial feast;
likewise, the enjoyment of the fruits of ritual action, as well as the enjoyment of female and male servants.
One should cause the protection of the monastery, its maintenance, and stone inscriptions to be made;
likewise, all the work pertaining to the deity and the retinue in the rites for the gods—
whatever ensures an inexhaustible livelihood according to the certainty of one's wealth.
One should not perform any other action with the thought that it is for the sake of the god Śeṣa.
Having gone to the temple or the house, the supreme abode is not seen;
however, having provided well-nourished enjoyments, one should perform the royal service.
Having divided [the offering] into three parts according to the extent of one's means,
one part is for the sake of Dharma, and two parts are the remainder for the deity.
By performing [the rites] in this sequence, one goes to the world of Śiva.
[Thus ends the chapter on the method for determining the manifestations born of yoga.]
Salutations to the illustrious Lord Somanātheśvara, accompanied by the illustrious Amṛtāmbā.
The Ritual for the Food Offering (Naivedya-vidhi):
Now I shall describe in detail the supreme ritual for the food offering.
[One should use] *homaśāli*, *mahāśāli*, and likewise *raktaśāli* rice.
There are white rice, black rice, and various other such distinct varieties in many ways.
Rice and all varieties of grains, barley, and wheat—
these are prescribed for all suitable [offerings], as is the remainder of the sacrificial oblation (havis).
Thirty śuktis make one vrīhi; a vyūha is said to be double that.
A kudhupa is likewise stated to be double, and two mudhus are equal to water.
It is said that two *vāris* make one *prastha*; make those two into one. Two of those are called an *ārdhaka*, and two of those are declared by Śiva to be a *havir*.
Two *śivas* are said to be one *droṇa*, or two of those are likewise defined; it is remembered that three *khāris* constitute a *bhāra*, according to the sequence.
One hundred bhāras is declared the best; fifty bhāras shall be the middling;
twenty bhāras the lowest; and ten bhāras the lowest of the low.
The *kṣudra* [measure] is two *bhāras* out of five *bhāras*;
it is called the *kalpabhāra*, and one should employ it according to one's capacity. One should prepare an *āḍhaka* of sacrificial oblation (*havir*), and half of that is said to be the *ruru*.
Half of that is said to be the *bali* offering; according to the rule "as much as one is able," the same applies to the attendants of Gaurī and the other Śaktis.
One should offer two *prasthas* for the sixteen images,
and one should present four parts of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) and two parts as well.
One part shall be the remainder; the remainder is for the offering of oblations and so forth. The eightfold sacrificial food (haviḥ) is said to consist of mung-bean rice and milk-rice (pāyasa).
Kṛsarānna, gulānna, śimbānna, yavānnaka, māṣānna,
and śuddhānna— these constitute the eightfold sacrificial oblation (havis).
One should avoid husked grain and mung beans, though they may be combined with coconut fruits.
Half a measure of rice, along with mung beans and a small amount of salt.
Thus it is said that rice mixed with meat is offered, as well as *kṛsarā* rice; likewise, plantains, molasses, cumin, and black pepper are included.
Combined with coconut meat and mixed with the juice of palasā, this is known as *āpipāna*; one should offer it at all times.
And for all [of them], one should provide a side-dish accompanied by finger-foods,
mixed with curd, honey, and ghee, and of five colors;
[one should give] one *prastha* of rice along with one fruit as a side-dish.
That, combined with a decoction of the throat (galasamyukta), together with black pepper and salt;
Cumin and coconut, combined with all kinds of side-dishes,
along with ghee, are ground together and called *śuddhopadaṃśa*.
Mango fruit, citron, and combined with tamarind fruit—
these, along with sour seasonings, black pepper, salt, and ghee.
One should especially avoid cumin, mustard, and fragrant grinding-stones; likewise, one should avoid food that is overcooked or undercooked.
A wise man should cook mustard seeds [as a remedy], for there are three kinds of skin diseases caused by insect bites.
Dry, parched, and unripened—unripened is of three kinds.
The breadfruit, the plantain, the mango, the bradīka,
the maṇḍa, the white hariphala, and likewise the fruit of the valli.
Kṣudramitiha, or even two niṣpāvas,
as well as śīgra, mārjāra, kāliṃ, timisī, and mātulaṅgaka.
It may have the form of a coconut or the fruit of the *raktāṅgasī*;
it has the root of the *karivallī* from the new region, and is dark with beautiful creepers;
it possesses beans upon beans and is endowed with fruits that ripen in ten days.
The wise know that the substance which is not conceited and is endowed with devotion is the true ground.
The root of the *vallī* is the *amīla*; the *karṇikā* has its root divided;
and that which has another root—among these, the wise man should provide the group of roots.
One should pacify other root-substances by means of devotion;
however, one should especially avoid the class of substances derived from *śakti*.
For those who are devoted to the eternal, unchanging [deity], one should offer [the substance] at a single time.
Marīca, sarṣapa, powdered jīraka, and coconut.
One should prepare this mixture with equal parts of these seasoned side-dishes;
having then blended ghee together with all the ingredients thoroughly combined.
A wise person should offer as a food-oblation (naivedya) that which possesses the six tastes and is mixed with ghee;
first, he should present the fruit of his agricultural labors to the God of gods.
A cook should prepare the food so that it is neither overcooked nor undercooked; one should especially avoid food that is excessively burnt or raw.
Having offered the great oblation (*mahāhavi*), one should place a leaf above the cloth—
either a *kadalī* leaf, a *palāśa* leaf, or a leaf from another milk-exuding tree.
One should offer the great sacrificial oblation (mahāhavis) into other pure vessels;
the oblation should consist of rice cooked with milk, sugar, and plantain fruit.
Having carefully poured ghee, or even just milk like curd,
one should offer it while reciting the mantra "devasya tvā" with devotion.
[One should also offer] pāṭalī, sugandhī, uśīra, and ela.
One should cause water to be offered first, and afterwards present it to Caṇḍeśa.
Having performed the purification of the floral remains, one should offer betel-leaf together with camphor,
nutmeg, black pepper, sesame oil, and areca nuts.
Thereafter, one should cause betel-leaf to be offered, accompanied by a small amount of lime-powder,
along with sandalwood, camphor, and musk for the mouth.
With a fan joined by mantra-songs and a gentle breeze,
one should touch the face of Rāvaṇa while seated upon the Himālaya.
When this is done, a mortal shall attain all sovereignty.
On Saturdays and Wednesdays, the wise man should consume fragrant oil when hungry.
[Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for the food offering (naivedya) born of yoga.]
Salutations to the venerable Lord Somanātheśvara, accompanied by the venerable Amṛtāmbā.
Regarding the fire-ritual:
I shall explain the procedure for the fire-ritual; listen with a one-pointed mind. A wise person should construct the sacrificial pit according to the rules for the characteristics of the pit.
Alternatively, in another manner, with white [materials] and water, there should be eight handfuls of oblations;
the characteristic of the *akṣahoma* is that it consists of eight cubits.
For ten thousand oblations, the sacrificial pit should be five cubits; for a thousand, three cubits;
and for two thousand, it should be one cubit, or exceeding five hundred cubits for a thousand-fold homa.
The *ratnamātra* measures one hundred [units], and the *dṛṣṭimātra* is half of that (fifty). From the *dṛṣṭimātra* onwards, the measurement of iron [rods] does not exceed eight cubits.
Construct it with three, two, or one rim, according to the characteristics of a sacrificial pit;
the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) should be one cubit in measure and provided with three finger-breadths.
Having established [the fires] in the south with five [fires], one should arrange the womb (yoni) in the north;
it should have three lines running eastward and northward, and be provided with the enclosures and the strewn grass.
In the eastern and western pits,
the wise practitioner, facing north, and in the others, facing east, should prepare the sacrificial ladle and spoon.
The spreading of grass is on the sacrificial ground below the altar; the thread is in the middle.
Starting from the southern enclosing stick, the [other] enclosing sticks are placed toward the east, excluding the northern one.
Having placed the *kūrca* grass-bundle upon that, one should then place fuel-sticks with their tips pointing upward;
the *kūrca* made of five, seven, eight, or nine *darbha* blades is positioned starting from the east.
One should fashion the sacrificial wood (paridhi) in the measure of the little finger;
the wise man should prepare the fuel-sticks (samidh) of twelve finger-breadths for the lowest grade.
A wise person should install the Brahmakūrca with six fingers and likewise the Viṣṇukūrca;
in the middle, however, he should establish the Rudrakūrca as the Trimūrti.

One should prepare all the bundles (*kūrca*) with three, five, five, and nine blades of grass; and the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should be made of four blades of darbha grass, eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length.
One should fasten the leaves of the Palāśa and Aśvattha trees, as well as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles;
one should bind the *pavitra* strainer with one, two, or three *darbha* blades respectively.
Three finger-breadths [in length] at the front and middle, half of that at the tip,
one should place those on the sides according to the measurement of the age.
This sacred thread (*pavitra*) is said to be joined at the base of the ring finger.
Having kindled the fire, one should offer oblations to Viha-ripa and to Maya.
Or one may take fire produced from a śrotriya’s house, or likewise that which arises from a sun-crystal,
or even from the friction of the little finger; the wise man should then sprinkle it with the water of Śiva and kindle the fire while holding fragrant wood.
One should arrange the spreading grass with its tips pointing eastward and its roots pointing toward the north.
Then the learned one, through the method of the supreme knowledge of Śiva, should cause the mantra of Śiva to be known:
[the deity] with two faces, one heart, four fields, and two nostrils.
He has two faces, eyes of excrement, is lame, and possesses seven hands;
he is adorned with three girdles, has three feet, and is endowed with seven tongues.
He is mounted upon a bull with four horns and has a radiance equal to the rising sun.
Having thus consecrated the fire as Śiva with the Śiva-mantra, the preceptor—
Having the form of an elder, with three eyes and four arms, with tawny eyes,
riding upon a bull, red in color, and wearing a white upper garment.
Supreme, having the nature of Śiva as fire with Śakti in his hand.
Resembling a mass of lightning, four-armed, with feet like those of a goat,
possessing two round faces with four horns, and having a blazing tongue and seven flames.
On her left hip, she wears a girdle of finest silk;
her right hand is turned back, while her left hand holds a vessel from which a stream of nectar flows, granting both the wish-granting boon and protection.
I shall describe each of those fires in their respective order: the Gārhapatya for householders, the Dakṣiṇāgni for the ancestors, and the Āhavanīya for the gods;
that which is performed as a sacrificial session (sattra) is proclaimed as the fire of the young, the middle-aged, and the elderly.
The installation of the Pratisthā images should be performed with the Bālāgni, and the festival (utsava) with the Yauvanāgni.
For the daily fire-oblation of the elders, one should proceed by way of both the left and right paths;
[the goddesses] Kālikā, Karālī, Vanoramā, and Sulohitā [are present].
Dhūmraparṇapulla, Nañ, Viśvarūpin, and Vilohita—
these are proclaimed as the powers (śaktis) of the state of Devilola.
Having placed the *brahmāṇanda* [vessel] on the right, one should carefully set down the *kūrca* and the flower;
having established Viṣṇu on the left, one should likewise place the *praṇītā* vessel in the northern direction.
One should place Paśupati in the northern pit, and likewise Īśāna and Miśra;
he has three eyes and four arms, and wears matted hair and a crown.
One should install these within the center of the pit, and likewise the group of eight Vasus on the outside.
Outside of that are the Maruts, and outside of that are the world-protectors (Lokapālas).
In the central fire-ritual, conjoined with the outer mantra, one should worship all the deities; this is remembered as the supreme oblation.

During the performance of this fire-sacrifice (*homa*), one should place all the deities— the guardians of the world (*lokapālas*) and the weapons (*astras*)— within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), specifically in the center of the pit.
One offers clarified butter with the *samidhāsadya* mantra;
having offered the *caru* with the *aghora* mantra, one should offer parched grain (*lāja*) with the *tatpuruṣa* mantra.
(3rd line) One should offer mustard seeds with the *īśāna* mantra, sesame with the *ekavaca* mantra, and having offered barley, [one should proceed].
The heart-mantra is drawn with the seventh mantra using palāśa and khadira wood.
The Aśvattha, the Vaṭa tree, the Nyagrodha, and the Plakṣa tree;
likewise the Apāmārga, the Śamī, the Bilva, and the Kapittha.
The *vaja* and the *būva* tree—thus is the fuel (*samidh*) described;
The drawing of lines on the sacrificial ground, the inspection, the establishment of the fire,
the spreading of the grass, the vessels, the sprinkling, and the declaration of the auspicious day (puṇyāha).
Having first worshipped Viṣṇu and Brahmā with the *kūrca* grass,
he should likewise worship the fire situated within the three *darbha* blades, as well as the sacrificial ladle and the enclosing sticks.
Then, having performed the sprinkling (pariṣecana) and circumambulation from left to right (pradakṣiṇa),
one should place pure water, ghee, and all other ritual substances.
One should perform the sprinkling with the mantra beginning with "adite 'nu... and prepare the mouth of the fire with the mantra beginning with "yukto vāhā...".
One should worship the deities, beginning with Mūrti, with their respective mantras;
at the conclusion of the ritual, one should offer the oblation of consciousness (cittāhuti) into the fire, which consists of the elements and the guardians of the realm.
One should perform all general rites, and then worship according to one's own specific rite;
furthermore, one should perform another sixteen-fold rite beginning with the union of the Ṛk verses.
One who has performed the purificatory rites of Śiva, possessing the five Brahmans and the six limbs, should perform the fire-oblation.
[Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for the fire-ritual in the *Pratiṣṭhātantra* of the *Yogaja* tradition.]
Salutations to Śrī Somanātheśvara, accompanied by Śrī Amṛtāmbā.
The Characteristics of the Fire-pit (Kuṇḍa):
Now I shall specifically describe the supreme characteristics of the fire-pit;
one should divide the center of the sacrificial pavilion into nine parts.
In the middle portion, one should construct an altar (vedi) with a height of one cubit;
the secondary altar (upavedi) should be made twice as wide and four finger-breadths [in height].
The height of the nine-deity [altar] should be six finger-breadths, or even more;
in the east it should be square, while in the southeast there is a yoni-shaped sacrificial pit.
In the south, there is a half-moon and a dancing triangle;
in the west, a circular pit, and in the northwest, a hexagon.
Let the gentle lotus-pool be octagonal in the direction of Īśa;
between Indra and Īśāna, construct the principal circle.
The *kuṇḍaka* is not square like all other *kuṇḍas*;
its measurement is proclaimed to range from eight cubits down to one handful (*muṣṭi*).
For all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), the measurement is one solid fist;
they may be provided with three tiers of rims or even just a single rim.
Beginning from the lower girdle, [the width] is two or three [units], and four [units];
the height is six finger-breadths; thus there is one girdle.
One should not fashion [the image] from womb to womb, nor should one cause Padmanābha to be made [in that way].
Having condensed it to the measure of a palm tree, one should arrange a lotus in the center.
The width of the tongue should be measured at six finger-breadths, or four finger-breadths,
or one finger-breadth, or even two finger-breadths.
Having thus performed the lotus-arrangement, one should place the fire-pit in its center;
upon the girdle, however, one should fashion the womb (yoni), measuring four finger-breadths in width.
The width of the foremost finger [of the base] is one finger, and its height is likewise one finger. Having divided the square into five parts, one should place one part at the front.
Having taken half of a quarter [of the side], one should exclude it from the outside;
from that corner, one should rotate another thread in the shape of a womb (*yoni*).
Having divided the width into nine parts and having placed a portion [of the cord] sequentially from top to bottom,
one should wrap the cord and rotate it to form a half-moon shape.
Having understood the counter-installation (kontranyāsa), the wise one, having performed the placement with a water-vessel, should stretch three threads;
this is declared to be the triangular pit (kaṇḍa).
Having made a square with nine [units], one should extend it toward the outer directions;
by rotating it, a dik-kuṇḍa is formed, which is suitable for all rites.
Having first fashioned it in the form of a square, one should then cause it to be made in the shape of a lotus,
provided with a pericarp and eight petals, and having the height of a lotus in the case of a large [image].
The wise man should measure the width of this square as four parts;
having measured one part for its breadth, he should then apply the cord.
One should rotate [the cord] from the white point toward the southeast; this is known as the circular pit (vṛttakuṇḍa).
Thus is described the characteristic of the pit in the absence of a square one.
Having taken half of the corner, one should not indeed form a corner;
thus there shall be an eight-cornered kuṇḍa for worship in all rites.
The fist and the arm [are formed] at the end of the eight hands;
[the shapes are] seven-sided, nine-sided, lotus-sided, and sixteen-sided.
The wise man should apply this logic and fashion all types of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas);
indeed, this measurement is declared to be the most excellent among all the pits.
Whatever is the measurement for the girdle, that is recorded as the measurement.
[Thus ends the chapter on the rules for the characteristics of the sacrificial pit according to the Yogaja school.]
Salutations to the glorious Lord Somanātheśvara accompanied by the glorious Amṛtāmbā.
(Second line) I shall now describe the rite of the Peace-Oblation (*śāntihoma*); listen with a one-pointed mind.
And likewise for the retinues of the deities beginning with Sadāśiva.
Within the enclosure, one should perform oblations with the names of the deities and so forth;
there, one should worship them twofold according to the sequence prescribed for worship.
This is declared to be the *śānti-homa*; one should offer oblations to all the deities.
This has been described as the *śānti-homa*; now hear about the *mūrti-homa*.
Within the inner mandala of the palace on its four sides, the wise one,
having prepared a square sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), should fashion a circular sacrificial mound in the northeast.
Following the very sequence of the fire-ritual (agnikārya), one should prepare the mouth of the fire;
Sadāśiva in the northeast, and the mantra of Raṃśa in the east.
One should offer oblations according to one's capacity with the Rudra-mantra in the south, the Viṣṇu-mantra in the west,
and the Brahmā-mantra in the north.
Thereafter, one should present the oblation (havis) and cause the Lord (Civa) to perform the ceremonial bath.
One should worship there twice as much and present the great oblation (mahāhavis).
This is declared to be the Mūrti-homa; now hear concerning the Diśā-homa.
Thus, from Indra to Śāna (Īśāna), these are the deities of the eight directions.
Having sprinkled the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) so that it is square on all sides,
one should perform all other remaining rites as prescribed for the officiant.
There, one should worship the deities of the directions and perform the oblation for the directions (diśāhoma).
This is called diśāhoma; now hear about the vāstuhoma.
In the center of the pavilion, prepare a leveled mound (maṇḍala) and place a vessel upon it;
having established the Vāstu-pitcher, one should worship the deities of the site (vāstu-devatās).
Having fashioned a square mandala measuring one cubit in size,
it may consist of eight times eight squares, or even nine times nine squares.
Having drawn [the mandala] with a cord, one should worship the deities beginning with Īśa;
having worshipped the deities beginning with Brahmā, one should worship those beginning with Carakī.
These forty-five should worship Vāsudeva.
Having worshipped the deities of the site, one should cause the offering to be given with the bali-mantra.
Then, having worshipped the deity of the site (vāstudeva), one should offer oblations to the gods in due order,
and likewise offer fuel-sticks with mantras beginning with their respective names.
At the proper time, perform the Vāstuhoma and the circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa);
likewise, perform the Vāstupūjā and the auspicious day rite (puṇyāha), as well as the water-offering for the site (vāstukumbhatoyaka).
This is declared to be the Vāstuhoma, which should be performed first at all times;
thus has the Homa been described, [to be offered] with their respective mantras into the heart.
[Thus ends the chapter on the Vāstu-homa, including the Śādi-homa and others, in the Yogaja-pratiṣṭhā-tantra.
(3rd line) Salutations to the venerable Somanātheśvara, accompanied by the venerable Amṛtāmbā.
Now I shall describe specifically the characteristics of initiation; listen to the definition of initiations.
For [in initiation] the knowledge of Śiva is bestowed (dīyate), and this impurity is destroyed (kṣiyate).
This word *dīkṣā* has been proclaimed as the bestower of both worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*).
The sevenfold Śaiva [tradition] has been indicated; now hear the division of the *miḍha*.
First is the *anādiśaiva*, and second is the *ādiśaiva*.
The third is indeed the Mandāśaiva, while the fourth is the Śaivaka.
The fifth is Antaraśaiva, while the sixth is Pravaraśaiva;
and the seventh is Antuśaiva—these are proclaimed as the divisions of Śaivism.
The Śaivas are said to be of seven kinds; hear now their distinctions from below. The Ādiśaiva is traditionally held to be among the Brahmins who have been initiated by Śiva.
And let those initiated into the five faces of the twice-born blow [the conchs]:
Kauśika, Kāśyapa, and Bhāradvāja in the north.
Parāśara and these five [sages] were initiated into the five faces;
the twice-born born of them shall not undergo initiation again.

One who is known as an Ādiśaiva and has been initiated (Ādikṣita) should perform the Śiva-pūjā and provide food for the four Vedas. Having eaten, he should offer the supreme [oblation] to Īśāna; even a twice-born man devoid of initiation may do so.
